table_content.text: Summary

The present report is the first addendum to the report of the Secretary-General on the proposed programme budget for 2027 under section 3, Political affairs, and contains information on the overall resource requirements of 36 special political missions authorized by the General Assembly and/or the Security Council.

The report describes the continued relevance and effectiveness of the contributions of special political missions to the prevention and resolution of violent conflict and to peacebuilding within an evolving global context and increasingly challenging operational environments. It further provides details on efforts undertaken and planned to strengthen a culture of efficiency in special political missions, including quantifiable savings achieved.
	The overall proposed resource requirements of special political missions for 2027 amount to $422,671,000 (net of staff assessment). The requirements include $3,259,100 to provide for the share of special political missions for the financing of the budget of the Regional Service Centre in Entebbe, Uganda, for the period from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027. Detailed information in respect of each special political mission is contained in three addenda to section 3, Political affairs (A/81/6 (Sect. 3)/Add.2, A/81/6 (Sect. 3)/Add.3, A/81/6 (Sect. 3)/Add.4) corresponding to three thematic clusters, with the resource requirements for the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan now incorporated into the report on thematic cluster III.

children.text: Introduction

Special political missions continued to play a vital role in the maintenance of international peace and security by contributing to the prevention and resolution of violent conflict and to peacebuilding in some of the world’s most complex contexts. Special political missions undertake a wide spectrum of critical functions, from engaging in preventive diplomacy and supporting the implementation of peace agreements, to assisting Member States in the promotion of human rights, enhancing the meaningful participation of women, and advancing the engagement of youth and other marginalized constituencies in political and peace processes. They also play a key role in strengthening the partnerships between the United Nations and regional and subregional organizations. Across all these areas, special political missions cooperate closely with United Nations development, human rights and humanitarian entities to implement integrated and effective responses.

The appropriation for special political missions for 2026 amounted to $536.1 million, representing a decrease of 22.6 per cent compared with the 2025 appropriation of $693.0 million, due primarily to the implementation of efficiency measures under the UN80 initiative, as well as the liquidation and closure of three missions: the United Nations Assistance Mission in Iraq (UNAMI), the United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) and the United Nations Mission to Support the Hudaydah Agreement (UNMHA).

The proposed budget for 2027 builds on the momentum of the UN80 initiative and aims to minimize resource growth, while continuing to pursue efficiencies where feasible. The proposed budget amounts to $422.7 million, representing a decrease of $113.5 million, or 21.2 per cent compared to the approved budget for 2026. The net decrease is attributable to: (a) a decrease of $121.5 million due the closure of the three missions noted in paragraph 2 above; and (b) an increase of $8.0 million attributable to the 36 continuing missions including an increase of $0.9 million for the share of special political missions in the cost of the Regional Service Centre (RSCE).  In terms of staffing, the proposed budget reflects an overall decrease of 89 posts and positions, including a reduction of four higher-level posts (D-1 and above).

The proposed budget reflects the collective effort of missions, supported by Headquarters, to maximize cost reductions and efficiency gains while maintaining effective mandate delivery. These efforts builds on a systematic process to enhance cost-effectiveness embarked upon by special political missions in the last few years, culminating in the launch in January 2025 of a strategic approach to a culture of efficiency. This initiative aims to transform discrete efficiency initiatives into a global, coherent, systematic, and consistent approach for all field missions. Efficiency initiatives resulted in actual savings of $16.8 million in 2025, while projected savings for 2026, initially estimated at $12.7 million (or 2.1 per cent of the approved 2025 budget) in the proposed budget, increased to reflect additional reductions of $96.3 million (or 15 per cent) under the revised estimates (A/80/400). The commitment to this culture of efficiency enables missions to reflect targeted efficiencies in their budget proposals for 2027 estimated at $14.7 million (or 3.6 per cent of the approved 2026 budget for these missions).

The full implementation of the programme budget continues to be impacted by the current liquidity situation. To operate within these liquidity constraints, cash conservation measures and hiring freezes have been implemented. For special political missions, the liquidity situation has also required that new and expanded mandates be accommodated largely within existing resources. This means that budget performance (and pattern of expenditures from the prior year) is no longer an indicator of mission requirements and implementation capacities.

In line with budgetary practices, any adjustments to the resource requirements emanating from additional mandates or changes in mandates will be presented to the General Assembly either as additional reports of the Secretary-General on estimates resulting from such changes of mandates, or as supplementary information or updates during the legislative review prior to the approval of budgets. Given the volatility of the security and operating environments of special political missions, should any changes from such environments significantly alter the planning assumptions and costing parameters applied in the current budget, and if such changes cannot be absorbed from existing resources, the consequent changes to either resource or staffing requirements will be brought to the attention of the General Assembly, as appropriate, in accordance with established practices and procedures, and pursuant to the financial regulations and rules of the United Nations.

As per established practice, the budget requirements of special political missions are presented as addenda to Section 3, Political affairs, of the proposed programme budget, and organized in three thematic clusters. Details of the individual missions are further presented in the following reports:
(a)	Thematic cluster I: special and personal envoys, advisers and representatives of the Secretary-General (A/81/6 (Sect. 3)/Add.2);
(b)	Thematic cluster II: sanctions monitoring teams, groups and panels, and other entities and mechanisms (A/81/6 (Sect. 3)/Add.3);
(c)	Thematic cluster III: regional offices, offices in support of political processes and other missions (A/81/6 (Sect. 3)/Add.4).

One change to the organization of reports for 2027 is with regard to the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA). Previously, the budgets of UNAMA and UNAMI (now closed and undergoing liquidation), despite both being part of thematic cluster III, were presented separately in standalone reports. That was the result of a practice introduced in 2007, at a time when UNAMA and UNAMI collectively represented two thirds of the total resources for special political missions. It is recalled that the General Assembly in its resolution 59/276 endorsed the recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions (A/59/569/Add.1, paras. 6 and 7) that the magnitude and complexity of large political missions, such as UNAMA and UNAMI, created new challenges in respect of effective consideration of resource requirements for special political missions and that while maintaining the overall benefits of consolidated reporting for most special political missions, the Secretary General should consider ways and means to present the budgets of large missions in a manner that would be more suitable for their size and complexity. To facilitate consideration, the Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions was of the view that thought should be given to reorganize the report on special political missions so that the missions would be presented in clusters on the basis of thematic or regional considerations, as appropriate. Reflecting the evolution of mandates and resource requirements over the past two decades, particularly following the closure of UNAMI in 2025, the proposed budget for UNAMA is now comparable in size to those of other large missions within thematic cluster III. Accordingly, the budget requirements for UNAMA are integrated into the report on thematic cluster III, beginning from the 2027 budget period. This integration enables a more harmonized structure and presentation across missions of similar magnitude and size, as well as a more enriched presentation of resource requirements for all missions under thematic cluster III.
B.	Status of the extension or renewal of mandates

C.	Discontinuing or discontinued missions

The mandate of UNAMI expired on 31 December 2025 pursuant to Security Council resolution 2732 (2024). The liquidation of UNAMI commenced on 1 January 2026 and is expected to be completed by 30 September 2026. Remaining liquidation activities will be transferred to the Department of Operational Support (DOS) in New York, while logistics and property management related activities will be undertaken by the United Nations Logistics Base (UNLB). The Kuwait Joint Support Office (KJSO) will be closed by 30 June 2026, with its clients transferred to RSCE.  Separately, on the issue of the missing Kuwaiti persons and missing Kuwaiti property not resolved upon termination of the mandate of UNAMI, the Security Council adopted resolution 2792 (2025) and requested the Secretary-General to appoint a senior representative to promote, support and facilitate efforts regarding the repatriation or return of all Kuwaiti and third-country nationals or their remains, as well as the return of Kuwaiti property, including the national archives. The new mission was established in 2026 under thematic cluster I, as previously reported in the revised estimates (A/80/6 (Sect. 3)/Add.7).

The mandate of UNTMIS is set to end on 31 October 2026 pursuant to Security Council resolution 2753 (2024). Its liquidation process will start on 1 November 2026 and be executed by a small residual team until 31 December 2026, jointly with the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS).

The mandate of UNMHA ended on 31 March 2026, pursuant to Security Council resolution 2813 (2026) adopted in January 2026. In the same resolution, the Security Council requested UNMHA to start the transfer of its residual functions to the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen. The liquidation budget of UNMHA and the proposal for transfer of residual functions to the Office of the Special Envoy were reported in the revised estimates (A/80/6 (Sect. 3)/Add.7). The liquidation process commenced on 1 April 2026 and is expected to be completed by 30 June 2026.
No resources are required for 2027 for the three discontinuing or discontinued missions.
Delivering mandates in an evolving global context
Performance information

The special envoys and advisers appointed by the Secretary-General, presented under thematic cluster I, continued to offer good offices and to facilitate negotiations with a view to brokering and implementing peace agreements. The Office of the Special Envoy for the Great Lakes Region supported the implementation of the Peace, Security and Cooperation Framework for the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Region, including through shuttle diplomacy and by providing support to the Regional Oversight Mechanism. The Special Envoy intensified engagements with regional and international stakeholders to prevent a regional spillover and maintain coherence and complementarity among the concurrent peace initiatives. Through sustained outreach, the Special Envoy helped ensure that African-led efforts were consistent with ongoing efforts under the Washington and Doha processes. The Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen engaged with a range of Yemeni stakeholders, with the aim of achieving de-escalation and maintaining the prospects for an inclusive, multitrack political process to end the conflict amid a significantly escalating situation. The Special Envoy for the Horn of Africa worked with regional leaders, Member States and partners to promote dialogue, advance preventive diplomacy and confidence‑building amid regional tensions, including through the establishment of structured engagement platforms.

The various sanctions monitoring teams, groups and panels, the Ombudsperson and the Focal Point presented under thematic cluster II continued to provide substantive support to the Security Council in the implementation of its respective sanctions regimes. By resolution  2819 (2026), the mandate of the Panel of Experts on Libya was renewed until 15 August 2027. In resolutions 2780 (2025) and 2804 (2025), the Council requested the Secretary-General to report on the implementation of the arms embargo on the high seas off the coast of Libya within 5 months of the adoption of the resolutions. The Secretary-General submitted his reports pursuant to those resolutions (S/2025/675 and S/2026/354, respectively. In addition, pursuant to resolution 2769 (2025), the Council authorized the frozen cash reserves of the Libyan Investment Authority to be invested in low-risk time deposits and in fixed financial instruments, subject to a notification and approval procedure by the Sanctions Committee established pursuant to resolution 1970 (2011) concerning Libya, and requested the Panel of Experts to assess the effect and performance of those investments in their annual final reports. The Security Council also mandated the Panel of Experts on Yemen to present two additional reports: the first regarding dual-use components and precursor chemicals and their direct or indirect sale, supply or transfer to Yemen, and the second on ways to improve information-sharing and flag State capacity to prevent vessels, suspected of violating resolution 2216 (2015), from entering Yemen. Pursuant to the process set forth in paragraphs 11 and 12 of Security Council resolution 2231 (2015), effective 27 September 2025, all provisions of resolutions 1696 (2006), 1737 (2006), 1747 (2007), 1803 (2008), 1835 (2008) and 1929 (2010) were re-applied in the same manner as they applied before the adoption of resolution 2231 (2015) on 20 July 2015. Accordingly, the Panel of Experts on the Islamic Republic of Iran was reinstated by the Security Council, and its 2026 budget was approved by the General Assembly in its resolution 80/254.

The United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia has implemented the adjustments to the mandate approved by Security Council resolution 2798 (2025), focused on verifying the implementation of the provisions of the Final Peace Agreement concerning comprehensive rural reform, the reintegration of former combatants, as well as their security, and that of communities in conflict-affected regions. The Mission accompanied the Government in the formulation of the rapid response plan adopted in October 2024 to accelerate the implementation of the Final Agreement, which includes the establishment of pacts between national and local authorities to accelerate the implementation of the development programmes with a territorial focus and to enhance their transformative potential in conflict-affected regions, as well as actions related to the comprehensive rural reform and security guarantees.

In Libya, in line with Libyan Political Roadmap, UNSMIL launched the Structured Dialogue with thematic groups on the economy, governance, security, as well as national reconciliation and human rights. Across the four tracks, the mission supported a series of meetings aimed at developing concrete recommendations. UNSMIL has also facilitated meetings between the Governance and Economy tracks of the Structured Dialogue and the relevant Berlin Process Working Groups in order for Libyans to convey first-hand their priorities and exchange views on international support needed to address critical reforms on strengthening governance.

In West Africa and the Sahel, UNOWAS led or supported several initiatives to prevent conflict, defuse election- and transition-related tensions, sustain peace and consolidate peacebuilding efforts. The Office continued efforts towards inclusive dialogue and open political processes, and intensified its support to nationally owned dialogue processes, including through engagement with civil society, youth and women. The Office worked closely with regional and subregional organizations to strengthen peace and security in the region and to safeguard regional integration. The mission continued to solidify its existing partnerships in the area of maritime safety and security in the Gulf of Guinea. In addition, the Office fostered cooperation between coastal States and Sahelian countries, enhancing collaborative efforts to counter the southward spread of terrorism and violent extremism conducive to terrorism.

In Haiti, BINUH developed the strategy requested through Security Council resolution 2743 (2024) in consultation with the government of Haiti, improving international support for a Haitian-led, Haitian-owned formula to restore democratic institutions, fostering participation of all sectors of Haitian society. The period saw the completion of the term of office of the Transitional Presidential Council and a peaceful handover of executive authority to the Council of Ministers on 7 February 2026.  BINUH provided advice and guidance to the Haitian Provisional Electoral Council on the main challenges of the electoral process. BINUH continued to mentor and advise the Haitian National Police (and the Penitentiary Administrative Directorate) on critical policing matters, including anti-gang and anti-kidnapping operations, intelligence, election security, judicial police, criminal investigations, weapons and ammunition management, gender, mainstreaming and gender equality, legal framework, and police integrity and oversight. In January 2026, the mandate of BINUH was renewed by the Security Council under resolution 2814 (2026), focusing on elections, disarmament, dismantlement and reintegration, human rights, and on eliminating the mandate on police while maintaining BINUH’s support to the judiciary and to helping to address prolonged pretrial detention, in addition to providing advisory support on the handling of high-risk individuals. In line with the provisions of paragraph (e) of the resolution 2793 (2025), UNSOH started providing, on a cost-recovery basis, mission support services to BINUH in support of the delivery of its mandate.

In Afghanistan, UNAMA continued to support dialogue between Afghan stakeholders, UNAMA and the international community on human rights, rule of law, governance and inclusion issues. Despite persistent restrictions on media freedoms, civic space and Afghans’ enjoyment of their human rights, most acutely affecting women, Afghans retained access to channels to express concerns and communicate priority needs, enabling their voices to inform discussions on protection of human rights, including the rights of women and girls, and advocacy for a coherent socio-economic, political and policy agenda. The Mission supported the counter-narcotics and private sector working groups under the Doha Process and facilitated the High-Level Coordination Forum and the Technical Level Coordination Forum with de facto ministries.
B.	Operating environment and key policy issues
1.	Women and peace and security

In line with the Secretary-General’s continued commitment to advocate for a minimum of onethird of women participants in mediation and peace processes, special political missions further advanced the full, equal and meaningful participation of women in peace and political processes and strengthened gender‑responsive conflict prevention, peacemaking and peacebuilding efforts. Gender advisers and gender focal points across special political missions continued to provide essential guidance to special representatives and envoys of the Secretary‑General, ensuring that gender analysis and multidimensional risk assessments were systematically integrated into political strategies, good offices engagements and reporting.

Following the launch of the Secretary-General’s Common Pledge for Women’s Full, Equal and Meaningful Participation in Peace Processes on 24 October 2024, efforts to broaden its uptake accelerated. As of December 2025, 43 mediating entities, including Member States, regional organizations and other mediation actors, had adopted the Pledge, which was initiated, developed and supported by DPPA to galvanize collective action to overcome persistent barriers to women’s participation. In Sudan, the Office of the Personal Envoy of the Secretary‑General facilitated civil society consultations on the protection of civilians, including a dedicated session with women’s groups, ensuring that women’s perspectives informed conflict‑resolution efforts and the Personal Envoy’s engagement with stakeholders.

The Office of the Special Envoy for the Great Lakes convened regular virtual coordination meetings with civil society organizations, women’s groups and youth representatives in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the wider Great Lakes region. These consultations provided timely gender‑responsive analysis during the rapid escalation of M23 hostilities in North Kivu beginning in January 2025 and the subsequent advances in South Kivu. Insights from women and local actors were systematically incorporated into the Office’s political, security and economic assessments, ensuring that local realities and gendered impacts directly informed reporting and recommendations.

The Mission of the Secretary-General’s Good Offices in Cyprus continued to support women’s organizations and women‑led initiatives, bringing together women and bicommunal women’s groups from across the island. Emphasizing the centrality of women’s participation in peacemaking, the Office sustained facilitation of the Technical Committee on Gender Equality and advanced efforts to operationalize and further implement elements of the Action Plan to ensure women’s full, equal and meaningful participation in the settlement process. In 2025, the membership of the Technical Committees reached gender parity, reflecting sustained advocacy and benchmarks established under the Action Plan. The Committee also co‑developed, together with the Technical Committee on Environment, a project on climate change and women in science, technology, engineering and mathematics, examining and addressing the disproportionate impacts of climate change on women.
2.	Youth and peace and security

In the context of growing geopolitical tensions and constrained resources, the youth, peace and security agenda remains an important framework across the United Nations system. During the reporting period, the Security Council held one meeting on youth, peace and security and subsequently adopted resolution 2807 (2025), reaffirming the positive role of youth, including young women, in conflict prevention, peacebuilding, sustaining peace and recovery, and emphasizing the importance of their full, effective and meaningful participation in peace and security efforts. The Council also recognized the significance of the world’s youth population as a potential driver of stability and resilience, while expressing concern that young people remain among those most adversely affected by armed conflict and instability.

Special political missions, uniquely positioned to advance the youth, peace and security agenda through their direct engagement with affected communities and established relationships with political actors and civil society organizations, continued to support youth participation in political and peace processes and to strengthen engagement with young women and men as agents of positive change. In March 2025, UNSMIL convened a workshop in Tripoli bringing together youth representatives and officials from the Ministries of Youth and Labour under its YouEngage strategy. Participants identified priorities for reducing community violence, including expanded vocational training, economic opportunities, psychosocial support and strengthened local governance. The United Nations Regional Centre for Preventive Diplomacy for Central Asia, through its Preventive Diplomacy Academy, continued to build the capacities of young leaders and support alumni-led community initiatives aimed at addressing drivers of tension and strengthening dialogue across communities in Central Asia and Afghanistan.

Special political missions also supported youth-led initiatives addressing structural drivers of conflict and promoting social cohesion. In Somalia, the Promoting Inclusive Action in Peacebuilding project in Marka District, supported by the Secretary-General’s Peacebuilding Fund, used the joint rehabilitation and management of irrigation canals as an entry point to address resource-related tensions between communities. Youth from different communities were trained as “peace agents” and played a leading role in establishing inclusive water governance committees. The initiative contributed to a significant reduction in disputes over water resources and strengthened cooperation among communities, demonstrating the important role young people can play in advancing local conflict prevention and inclusive governance. In Afghanistan, amid continued restrictions on civic space, UNAMA conducted a series of youth consultations across the country in 2025 to facilitate engagement between Afghan youth and the United Nations. The consultations culminated in a Youth Roundtable held on 25 September 2025 that brought together participants from all regions of the country and ensured gender-balanced participation, including young women. Participants discussed issues affecting young people and shared perspectives on priorities and concerns regarding their future.
3.	Electoral assistance

During the reporting period, special political missions continued to provide electoral assistance to Member States where mandated or requested. In her capacity as the General Assembly-mandated focal point for electoral assistance, the Under-Secretary-General for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs receives requests aimed at supporting and strengthening the capacities of national electoral institutions. United Nations technical assistance and capacity-building were delivered in an integrated manner and, in many cases, alongside preventive diplomacy and conflict prevention efforts to foster consensus on electoral legal frameworks, promote inclusion and non-discrimination, and encourage broad participation. Missions with electoral mandates continued to ensure that electoral assistance activities were guided by the principles of respect for sovereignty, national ownership and sustainability, while promoting the participation of women, youth, persons with disabilities and other marginalized groups.

In Libya, municipal council elections remained an ongoing process spanning 2025 and continuing into 2026. Pursuant to Security Council mandates, the United Nations is providing technical and advisory support to the High National Elections Commission through UNSMIL and the integrated UN electoral support team. This includes support to voter registration systems, operational preparedness and institutional capacity, as well as assistance to the UN-facilitated political roadmap and Structured Dialogue aimed at resolving legal, institutional and governance obstacles to credible presidential and legislative elections.

In Somalia, UNTMIS provided technical assistance to the newly established National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission, including legal, operational, logistical and training support. The Mission assisted the Commission on the electoral legal framework, planning, logistics, candidate nomination procedures, women’s representation and ballot design. On 25 December 2025, the Commission conducted its first one-person, one-vote district elections in Banadir, Mogadishu, with technical support from UNTMIS. The Mission also delivered training sessions for civil society organization leaders in the Federal Member States on temporary special measures, electoral systems and electoral observation, and continued to provide technical advice for forthcoming district, state and federal electoral processes.

In Iraq, on 11 November 2025, Iraq held its sixth parliamentary elections since 2005 with the support of UNAMI. The elections took place in a generally peaceful environment, with no major irregularities reported, reflecting Iraq’s significant democratic progress. This marked the final electoral event supported by UNAMI. Over more than two decades, UNAMI assisted with 17 electoral processes, including six federal legislative elections, provincial polls, and elections in the Kurdistan Region. UNAMI’s support focused on strengthening the Independent High Electoral Commission, enhancing institutional capacity and procedures, and promoting trust through dialogue, inclusion, and transparency. In 2025, UNAMI’s electoral assistance continued to operate at the intersection of preventive diplomacy, technical advice, human rights, gender equality, and development.
4.	Safety and security

The majority of special political missions continue to operate in security environments which are characterized by their volatility and unpredictability, particularly within the context of highly complex local and regional events. Many missions deliver their mandates in areas of high-intensity military conflict or where the risks of terrorism, kinetic activity by armed groups, social unrest and high criminality require active mitigation, while in areas of relative stability, the situation may evolve to present serious safety and security threats.

In many locations mission personnel, assets and premises remain at considerable risk from security threats including through being in proximity to incidents where the Organization is not the intended target. In Haiti, BINUH operates in an environment where gang violence and criminality continue to affect international support to the country, while missions in Yemen again saw significant military activity in areas they operate. Other missions across countries including Afghanistan, Iraq, Somalia and Syria also continued to face evolving security challenges related to their day-to-day activities as well as to the drawdown of their presence in some cases.

While host Governments bear primary responsibility for the security of mission personnel, some lack the capacity to provide adequate protection, therefore special political missions continued to adapt to local conditions, undertaking active measures to ensure the continued effective delivery of their mandates and fulfilment of their operational objectives. In support of this approach, missions have adopted robust security measures, guided by ongoing and systematic risk management processes. These are founded on a process of continuous risk assessment, adjustment of profile and presence, along with the implementation of proactive mitigation measures, including through deploying United Nations armed civilian security personnel, guard units and other security modalities where necessary.

In all contexts the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs (DPPA) and the missions’ leadership work closely with the Department of Safety and Security (DSS) and other entities to review and refine risk management strategies, including mitigation measures as needed, in order to minimize disruption to mandate implementation, including in support of the deployment of expert panels supporting Security Council committees.
C.	Evaluation activities

DPPA continued to support evaluations and audits, including those conducted by external oversight bodies such as the Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS), the Joint Inspection Unit (JIU), and the Board of Auditors as well as its own internal evaluations. When relevant, key findings, recommendations and lessons learned arising from these evaluations were shared with special political missions to strengthen and inform their mandate implementation, and have been factored in the programme plan for the upcoming period.

In 2025, OIOS completed an evaluation of conflict specific special political missions under thematic cluster I to assess the relevance, effectiveness and coherence of their contributions to mitigating the risk of violent conflict. The evaluation concluded that these missions were uniquely positioned to convene stakeholders and facilitate dialogue, drawing on their perceived legitimacy, credibility and impartiality. Missions engaged a broad range of actors, including parties to conflict, geopolitical stakeholders, intergovernmental bodies and civil society, and employed diverse modalities to support political processes in complex and evolving contexts. The evaluation also found that missions effectively leveraged partnerships within the United Nations system and with external stakeholders to expand the scope and reach of their activities. At the same time, the evaluation identified areas for improvement, notably the need to strengthen strategic planning to better respond to evolving mandates and operating environments, enhance inclusivity to support broader social buy‑in and the sustainability of peace processes, and improve inter‑mission collaboration by making more systematic use of existing information‑sharing mechanisms.

In 2025, DPPA provided support to the OIOS exercise on strengthening the role of evaluation and the application of evaluation findings on programme design, delivery and policy directives as well as the evaluation of the mandate implementation by UNAMA. Mission-specific evaluation activities are described, as applicable, under the specific missions in the three addenda to section 3, Political affairs (A/81/6 (Sect. 3)/Add.2, A/81/6 (Sect. 3)/Add.3, A/81/6 (Sect. 3)/Add.4).
D.	Lessons learned from the closure of missions and transition planning

DOS continues to systematically capture and apply lessons learned from mission closures and transitions to strengthen future planning and execution. Insights drawn from completed and ongoing closures are analyzed and fed back into policy, guidance, and operational frameworks, ensuring that institutional knowledge is retained and applied consistently. These lessons directly inform practical guidance materials, including the Senior Mission Leadership Closure Guide, as well as associated standard operating procedures, tools, and checklists. They are also embedded in tailored training programmes and learning modules for senior leadership, planners, and operational staff, helping to build capacity, mitigate risks, and promote orderly, cost-effective, and well-coordinated mission drawdowns across the Secretariat.
From 2025 to early 2026, lessons learned from past mission transitions and closures were integrated into the planning processes of the liquidation of UNAMI, UNTMIS and UNMHA.

In Iraq, in line with Security Council resolution 2732 (2024) and the Secretary-General’s Transition and Liquidation Plan (S/2024/966), UNAMI continued to implement its mandate and drawdown during its final year. By 2 April 2026, UNAMI formally handed over all of its premises to the Government of Iraq following environmental remediation, asset verification and the repatriation of the United Nations Guard Unit.. UNAMI will continue to undertake liquidation related tasks remotely, until 30 September 2026, after which all residual liquidation activities will be transferred to DOS.

In order to help preserve gains and sustain peace, in cooperation with Iraqi counterparts, UNAMI worked with the United Nations country team and relevant agencies, funds and programmes on a set of thematic priorities that could continue to be advanced in the post-mission phase. This included electoral assistance, as the Mission had worked in support of the Independent High Electoral Commission, which managed the smooth and effective conduct of the November 2025 Council of Representatives election.

To ensure uninterrupted security at the United Nations Integrated Compound in Baghdad, a new unarmed guard force recruited jointly by DSS and the United Nations Development Programme assumed full-time access and internal control duties on 15 December 2025, replacing UNAMI’s guard unit personnel.

Drawing from lessons learnt from past United Nations transitions, UNAMI undertook extensive efforts to support career transitions for staff separating from the Mission, including upskilling, reskilling, and other professional development initiatives. Its Training Unit, in close collaboration with the Capacity Development and Operational Training Service within DOS, organized multiple training events and hosted four job fairs – one each in Baghdad, Erbil, Mosul and Kirkuk – with dozens of private sector employers, attracting over 350 United Nations staff and personnel.

The United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework for Iraq for 2025-2029 was signed on 25 December 2025 by the Minister of Planning and the United Nations resident coordinator. In line with recommended practice, the framework incorporates residual tasks previously mandated to UNAMI, such as electoral assistance, human rights, women, peace and security, and climate security, and further aligns with the national priorities of economic diversification, social protection, climate and water resilience, good governance and the rule of law.

In Somalia, the phased two-year transition of the United Nations presence, as outlined in resolution 2753 (2024), continued to progress during the reporting period. The handover of responsibilities under the first phase (ended 31 October 2025) has been completed. A roadmap for the second and final phase of the transition, jointly developed by the Federal Government of Somalia and the United Nations, was endorsed by the Security Council in its resolution 2809 (2025) and is currently under implementation. The drawdown of UNTMIS is scheduled to be completed by 31 October 2026.

Following the adoption of the road map for the second phase of the transition, the Joint Technical Committee is meeting quarterly to monitor progress on all remaining UNTMIS tasks to be fully transitioned to the Federal Government, the country team and other stakeholders, and to address challenges and ensure that the implementation of the road map remains on track for the conclusion of the UNTMIS mandate by 31 October 2026.

This work has informed the development of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework for Somalia for the period 2026-2030, which has been aligned to support the implementation of the country’s national transformation plan. UNTMIS will support joint resource mobilization strategies of the joint Federal Government of Somalia and the United Nations country team through the use of existing pooled funds such as the Somali Joint Fund and the Secretary-General’s Peacebuilding Fund, as well as by reaching out to international financial institutions, other donors, and the Somali private sector.

The Council requested in its resolution 2786 (2025) a review of UNMHA with a view to delivering further efficiencies and structural coherence and coordination across United Nations missions in Yemen. After the arbitrary detention of dozens of UN national personnel (73 since 2021), the United Nations had to significantly narrow the operating environment for staff across Houthi-controlled areas as a mitigating measure to ensure staff safety and security. In response to heightened security risks in Houthi-controlled areas, in October 2025, UNMHA international staff temporarily relocated to Government-controlled areas, along with other United Nations international staff, from Houthi-controlled areas.

In its resolution 2813 (2026), the Council extended the mandate of UNMHA for a final two-month period until 31 March and requested that UNMHA residual tasks be transferred to the Office of the Special Envoy for Yemen. In February 2026, both UNMHA and the Office of the Special Envoy for Yemen jointly developed a transition plan and initiated the gradual handover of UNMHA’s core residual tasks to the Office of the Special Envoy for Yemen. A joint delegation from UNMHA and the Office of the Special Envoy for Yemen met with members of the Redeployment Coordination Committee in Hudaydah. Discussions focused on joint achievements by the Redeployment Coordination Committee, residual tasks and transition arrangements to the Office of the Special Envoy for Yemen. UNMHA and the Office of the Special Envoy for Yemen reiterated the commitment of the United Nations to continue supporting the implementation of the Hudaydah Agreement and the importance of sustained communication and cooperation in support of stability in Hudaydah and in Yemen. The delegation also met with Houthi de facto authorities in Sana’a, further developing the necessary transition arrangements, and preparing for the next phase of their partnership. UNMHA has also engaged with the United Nations country team, local authorities and other key actors to ensure a smooth handover to the Office of the Special Envoy for Yemen.
III. 	Operational effectiveness and responsible stewardship – A.	Integration of services in the Regional Service Centre in Entebbe, Uganda

Established in July 2010, the Regional Service Centre in Entebbe (RSCE) provides administrative, financial, procurement, logistical and information and communication technology (ICT) services to peacekeeping operations, special political missions and other client entities. The Centre also provides residual administrative and liquidation support to closed and liquidating missions, thereby safeguarding the Organization’s fiduciary responsibilities beyond mandate closure. Through the application of standardized processes, economies of scale and strengthened internal controls, the RSCE enables client entities in the discharge of their mandate while promoting efficiency, accountability and continuity of operations.

In 2026, in line with the recommendation of the ACABQ as endorsed by the General Assembly in resolution 78/294, RSCE adopted a phased, risk-based approach to assume responsibility for the provision of services to current client entities previously supported by the Kuwait Joint Support Office (KJSO). The full operational integration of these clients into RSCE service delivery arrangements will take effect on 1 July 2026, concurrent with the operational closure of KJSO. The transition was coordinated under the leadership of the Department of Operational Support and guided by dedicated governance and transition management arrangements, with a view to ensuring operational readiness, service continuity and an orderly transfer of responsibilities. The Secretariat considers this integration a significant milestone in its efforts to strengthen, standardize and consolidate shared service delivery, in line with the Secretary-General’s reform agenda and the requests from the General Assembly on centralized support functions.

As of 1 July 2026, RSCE will support 33 active client entities with combined annual budgets of approximately $4.3 billion. The transfer of KJSO clients will result in an increase in the number of active clients receiving full services. This level of service activities underscores the Centre’s critical role in enabling the effective and compliant implementation of mandates financed under both peacekeeping and regular budget resources.

In addition to supporting active mandates, the RSCE continues to perform residual liquidation functions for previous client missions whose mandates expired in previous periods, including the United Nations Integrated Transition Assistance Mission in Sudan (UNITAMS), the United Nations Integrated Peacebuilding Office in Guinea-Bissau (UNIOGBIS), where certain administrative support processes remain.  The Centre is also assuming responsibility for residual liquidation support for the United Nations Investigative Team to Promote Accountability for Crimes Committed by Da’esh/Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant (UNITAD), UNAMI, and UNMHA, all of which transitioned from the KJSO to the RSCE.

The proposed budget for RSCE for the 2026/27 period (see A/80/611) is currently under consideration by the General Assembly at the second part of its resumed eightieth session. In that budget, resources in the amount of $45,155,400 are proposed by the Secretary-General for the maintenance of the Centre for the period from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027, to be apportioned on a pro rata basis among the budgets of the Centre’s active client peacekeeping operations, as well as special political missions financed under section 3, Political affairs, of the regular budget. The Advisory Committee recommended that the proposed resources be increased by $756,200, from $45,155,400 to $45,911,600, for the maintenance of the Centre for the 12-month period from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027 (A/80/604/Add.4, para. 56). Towards this end, an amount of $3.3 million has been included in the proposed programme budget for 2027, representing the share of special political missions. This provision will be subject to a final adjustment to be made in accordance with the decision to be taken by the Assembly in the context of the budget of RSCE for the 2026/27 period, which is expected by the end of June 2026.

With regard to the Advisory Committee’s observation that the provision of a full suite of services to clients previously receiving limited services should be reviewed for possible streamlining (A/80/7/Add.10, para. 56), the Secretariat underscores that the RSCE is fully positioned to provide the complete range of non-location dependent services to all former KJSO clients.
B.	Aligning human resources and capabilities with operational requirements

Within the broader context of the UN80 initiative, improving efficiency, realigning functions and optimizing the way the Organization work are core considerations when undertaking workforce planning. For delivering on these expectations, having strategic workforce capabilities continue to be reinforced throughout the Organization. For example, the key capabilities for a UN 2.0, including data expertise, innovation capacity, digital dexterity and strategic foresight and leveraging behavioural science are priorities, along with strengthening capabilities in strategic communications. New generic job profiles covering these capabilities have been developed or are under development.

Proposals for reclassification and reassignment of existing functions in missions using these new profiles, especially when leveraging opportunities from upcoming retirements to create more junior-level posts to rejuvenate the workforce, are vital elements in advancing a workforce transformation. Particular attention is also paid to reducing the number of high-level posts (D-1 and above), with the proposed budget for 2027 comprising: the abolishment of one USG in Support to the implementation of Security Council resolution 1559 (2004), one D-1 in the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia and one D-1 in BINUH; and the downward reclassification  of one D-1 post to the P-5 level in the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Syria.

Efforts continue to ensure that human resources policies are responsive to the needs of entities with a field presence. Specifically, the Office of Human Resources develops and revises administrative issuances, streamlined policies and procedures to respond to the needs of field entities and provides authoritative policy interpretation and advice on all human resources policies applicable to field entities, including in emergency and crisis situations, as well as during downsizing and reduction of staff exercises. The Office remains actively engaged in the work of the Human Resources Network Standing Committee on Field Duty Stations and the tripartite Working Group for the Review of Conditions of Life and Work in Field Duty Stations of the International Civil Service Commission (ICSC), which monitor matters related to the conditions of service of staff in the field, including rest and recuperation, danger pay, hardship classification and non-family designation of duty stations. As part of the Office’s participation in ICSC discussions, ongoing reviews are carried out for key field entitlements, including hardship allowance, non-family service allowance, mobility incentive, relocation package, danger pay and security evacuation allowance, as well as the methodology for setting post adjustment in field duty stations. The Office is actively engaged in the comprehensive review of the United Nations common system compensation package being conducted by ICSC pursuant to 77/256 A-B, which includes a full review of the compensation package for staff in field locations. The Office also conducts periodic salary surveys to establish and update salary scales for staff in locally recruited categories in field duty stations.
Promoting national capacities

Encouraging the use of national capacities has been a core area of focus in human resources management in special political missions. In line with the request of the General Assembly in its resolutions 61/276 and 66/264 for greater utilization of national staff, and through the guidance provided in the workforce planning nationalization guide issued in December 2021, special political missions reviewed their staffing requirements prior to the submission of the budget to determine the feasibility of nationalization, commensurate with the requirements of the missions and their respective mandates.

According to the workforce planning nationalization guide, when identifying opportunities for nationalization, special political missions use the following criteria: (a) identification of vacant international posts and positions, including United Nations Volunteer positions, which could be considered for conversion to national posts or positions; (b) in the case of any changes in mandate, determination of whether the function remains necessary to meet the objectives of the mission and maintain the international character of the operation; (c) assessment of whether there might be a perception of conflict of interest for the function; (d) determination of whether the function requires regular movement across international borders or lines of conflict; (e) determination of whether the function has security-related requirements that prohibit specific categories of staff; and (f) determination of the availability of talent in the local labour market, including the required knowledge and skills. The rate of nationalization is therefore dynamic and can be affected if there is a lack of qualifications in the local labour market, which tends to occur in conflict-affected areas where the local education system and pool of qualified candidates may have been disrupted.

The conditions and criteria for nationalization outlined above are further assessed against each mission’s operational context. Missions were encouraged to ensure that national staff are empowered and skilled to carry out the implementation of the mandate while ensuring that the international character of the mission is maintained.

Special political missions continued to make steady progress in the nationalization of posts . For 2027, it is proposed that two posts be nationalized in the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia and one post in UNSMIL. In addition, eight additional national posts (six National Professional Officer and two Local level) are proposed to be established in UNSMIL reflecting the Mission’s efforts towards the promotion of national capacity for the delivery of its critical mandated activities, and one Local level in the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia, as indicated in table 1.

children.text: Gender parity and geographical representation

The Organization is advancing efforts to achieving gender parity, guided by the principles of merit and fairness in all selection processes. Efforts are ongoing, with focus on strengthening recruitment, particularly through a proactive outreach, among other efforts. While financial constraints continue to cause temporary hiring restrictions, the Organization remains committed to pursuing existing efforts and expanding targeted engagement, especially for field-based roles in special political missions. Outreach strategies are being refined to maintain momentum and ensure a steady pipeline of diverse talent.

Improving living and working conditions in field duty stations remains a critical priority for the recruitment and retention of women and continues to be advanced through more targeted and practical interventions. Efforts are focused on strengthening the implementation of the Field-specific Enabling Environment Guidelines for the United Nations System, including by strengthening more consistent implementation across duty stations and promoting measurable improvement in safety, flexibility and inclusive workplace practices. Particular attention is being given to reinforce organizational culture and leadership accountability, informed by the results of the 2024 staff engagement survey, to address persistent gaps in workplace experience across field settings. At the same time, dedicated efforts are under way to strengthen workforce resilience, including through enhanced support for mental health and well-being of all staff, preventive psychosocial measures and the expansion of tools and guidance for managers to better support staff serving in hardship duty stations, who face heightened stressors and operational challenges.

The Secretariat remains committed to accelerating progress towards equitable geographical distribution in posts subject to geographical distribution and to promoting as wide a geographical basis as possible in the recruitment of staff for non-geographical posts, including those in special political missions and peacekeeping operations. Achieving equitable geographical distribution and greater geographical representation requires sustained and deliberate action, particularly in light of low applicant volumes from un- and underrepresented Member States, systemic challenges and legacy recruitment patterns.

As highlighted in the report of the Secretary-General on the Implementation of human resources management reforms: outlook for 2026–2029, structural issues in the staff selection system continue to hinder faster progress towards the equitable geographical distribution goal. In response, the Secretariat is advancing reforms to strengthen its staff selection framework. The implementation of the staff selection 2.0 initiative is progressing, aimed at enhancing the efficiency, transparency and consistency of recruitment processes and supporting more objective and skills-based selection decisions. Concurrently, the Secretariat has recalibrated its talent attraction approaches, including through the development of purposeful partnerships with Member States, universities and professional networks, with a focus on expanding outreach and translating such efforts into sustained improvements in geographical representation. These efforts are aimed at positioning the United Nations as an employer of choice and at cultivating diverse talent pipelines to meet both current and future workforce needs. This forward-looking approach is designed to ensure a continuous flow of qualified candidates and to strengthen workforce readiness. While substantive change will require time, benefits from this approach are already anticipated in the short to medium term. The Secretariat underscores the importance of adequate resources to sustain and scale talent outreach initiatives. Additional investments would enhance the Secretariat’s capacity to engage meaningfully with Member States and to implement outreach activities in support of equitable geographical distribution.
Generic job openings recruitment panels

Recruitment from global rosters remains a critical enabler for timely and high-quality staffing of civilian positions in special political missions.  Under the new staff selection system policy promulgated through the administrative instruction ST/AI/2025/2, the building and management of rosters is reinforced as the Secretariat’s primary mechanism for ensuring that qualified, gender-balanced, geographically diverse and multilingual personnel are readily available for rapid deployment to support mission mandates. Expert panels, which play a central role in the establishment and maintenance of global rosters for international recruited positions, are normally comprised of at least three members, including two subject matter experts at the same or higher level of the job opening, at least one woman and one member from outside the originating work unit. This composition enhances impartiality, consistency and the overall integrity of the assessment process. Expert panels, which mirror the constitution of assessment panels, will continue to convene in 2027 to assess and recommend candidates applying to Generic Job Openings in support of the roster-based recruitment by field missions. By centralizing the assessment function, the panels reduce the administrative burden on individual hiring managers while supporting the Human Resources Services Division of the Department of Operational Support in conducting high quality- and standardized evaluations. Roster selections continue to demonstrate their operational value as a fast-track recruitment modality: in 2025, 70 per cent of selections for international positions (Field Service level 4 to D-1) in field missions (special political missions and peacekeeping operations) were from rosters, compared with 37 per cent in the global Secretariat.

In 2027, through its Human Resources Services Division and in collaboration with roster-building partners across the Secretariat, DOS will continue to manage generic job openings across networks to ensure that the global rosters remain current diverse, and responsive to projected civilian staffing demands in special political missions. These efforts are further supported by enhanced assessment modalities, continued improvements to the Secretariat’s recruitment platform, and strengthened data-driven operational workforce planning methodologies to reinforce the timely deployment of high-quality personnel in support of evolving mission mandates.
Strengthening coherence and collaboration between pillars in special political missions

Depending on the context of the country and mission, the Deputy Special Representatives of the Secretary-General may have triple functions to perform, also serving as resident coordinators and humanitarian coordinators. Five special political missions, namely UNTMIS, the Office of the United Nations Special Coordinator for Lebanon, UNSMIL, BINUH, and UNAMA include Deputy Special Representatives of the Secretary-General, or Deputy Special Coordinators, who have the triple functions and serve also as resident coordinators and humanitarian coordinators in complex, multidimensional contexts. These deputies constitute the link between the political work of the special political mission and the United Nations entities implementing development and humanitarian activities in coordination with the mission. As Resident Coordinator, the incumbent is responsible for coordinating operations and activities relating to the United Nations country team and United Nations development activities, for ensuring that the activities of the United Nations country team are aligned with national priorities, as captured in United Nations cooperation frameworks, for providing oversight and transparency on joint activities of the United Nations country team and for mobilizing partnerships and financing in support of country efforts towards the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. The office of the resident coordinator supports those functions. As Humanitarian Coordinator, the incumbent is responsible for coordinating humanitarian plans and operations and for maintaining links with Governments and other parties, donors and the broader humanitarian community. The salaries and common staff costs related to the posts of Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General, Resident Coordinator and Humanitarian Coordinator are budgeted at 50 per cent of the total cost in the 2027 budgets of the respective special political missions, pursuant to General Assembly resolutions 59/296 and 72/279, with the other 50 per cent funded through the Development Coordination Office. In line with Security Council resolution 2594 (2021), the Secretariat continues to strengthen coherence and collaboration between the respective pillars in mission settings.

Appropriately sized and dedicated capacity in the mission structure is required to support the Deputy Special Representatives, Resident Coordinators and Humanitarian Coordinators in carrying out their cross-pillar function within the respective mission and to provide sufficient support for their role in coordinating the work of the various units reporting to them. Where needed, the Secretariat will apply the two criteria of its policy in ascertaining the level of support capacity for the Deputy Special Representatives of the Secretary-General, Resident Coordinators and Humanitarian Coordinators: (a) the number of units reporting to them; and (b) the number of substantive mandate points assigned to the office (see A/79/6 (Sect. 3)/Add.1, para. 79).
C.	Continued efforts to improve operational effectiveness
Air operations

The Secretariat has taken measures to seek efficiencies and enhance the utilization of air fleets, with guidance provided to inform staff in field missions with the requisite technical and operational oversight. The portfolio of standby air solutions, which include charter agreements, air ambulance services, aircraft services under letters of assist and other short-term agreements, is aimed at increasing the Secretariat’s agility and responsiveness in logistics by addressing, among other things, urgent requests for ad hoc requirements, and at providing improved, efficient and timely support.

In 2026, total approved resources for air operations for the 36 special political missions amount to $27.6 million, with planned utilization of approximately 2,903 flight hours (2,203 for fixed-wing aircraft and 700 for rotary-wing aircraft). For 2027, resources in the amount of $22.4 million are proposed for a total of 2,016 flight hours (1,406 for fixed-wing aircraft and 610 for rotary-wing aircraft). This represents a decrease of $4.7 million, or 17 per cent, in proposed resources, and a reduction of 887 flight hours, or 30.6 per cent, compared with 2026. Six missions (Office of the Special Envoy for Yemen, UNOWAS, UNSMIL, the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia, BINUH and UNAMA) account for 99.4 per cent of the total projected air operations requirements for 2027.  The decrease in requirement is the result of: (a) the downsizing of the aviation fleet in the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia through the discontinuation of the rental and operations of the fixed-wing aircraft and the reduction of one rotary-wing aircraft, owing to operational adjustments and optimization of fleet utilization; (b) reduced requirements in UNSMIL and UNAMA due to a decrease of flight hours in line with historical utilization rates; and (c) a review of the BINUH’s air operations arrangements following the deployment of UNSOH and the arrangements with UNSOH to utilize its air capabilities on a cost recovery basis in BINUH. The decrease is offset in part by increased requirements for the Office of the Special Envoy for Yemen reflecting a full-year provision in 2027, compared with nine months in 2026, following the transfer of UNMHA air operations contracts to the Office of the Special Envoy effective 1 April 2026.
Travel

The total resources proposed for official travel amount to $9.8 million, reflecting a decrease of $56,100, or 0.6 per cent, compared with the approved budget for 2026. While the reduction is modest, this reflects a level carefully considered after multiple years of reductions to resources under official travel. The travel plans are based on the principle that official travel will be undertaken only where it cannot be substituted by other means of communication, including videoconferencing. For the sanctions monitoring teams, groups and panels, the proposed budget for official travel of staff for 2027 takes into account the frequency of travel by the Chairs of relevant sanctions committees to countries and regions relevant to their respective sanctions regime, which requires support from Secretariat staff. The proposed budget for all sanctions expert groups or panels not based in New York provides for one trip by one Secretariat staff member to the relevant region to assist the Chair and/or the group or panel, as well as two trips by one staff member to assist the group or panel during the drafting of interim or midterm and final reports. In addition, the proposed budget for three of the groups or panels that are not based in New York includes one more trip by two Secretariat staff to a country relevant to the sanctions regime to conduct Security Council-mandated sanctions assessment missions.

The programme plans of the special political missions, as presented in the proposed programme budget under the thematic clusters, provide further information, when applicable, on how special political missions have incorporated good practices and increased the use of technology in their work, while also reflecting upon the challenges experienced where technology meets its limits and in-person travel is needed to meet demand and fill coverage gaps. Travel to provide good offices and mediation, conduct fact-finding, investigation and monitoring activities, verify compliance and conduct outreach, as well as provide training or capacity-building to national and local partners, remains an indispensable tool in carrying out the work of the special political missions in 2027.

With respect to the performance of special political missions against the 16-day advance purchase policy, the Secretariat is following the observations and recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions with respect to the need to put measures in place to enhance performance. The overall performance of all special political missions improved from 39 per cent in 2024 to 50 per cent in 2025, maintaining a sustained positive trend since 2019 (18 per cent).  Out of 37 missions in 2025, three achieved 100 per cent and majority of the remaining (22 missions) showed improved performance compared to 2024. This improvement reflected efforts across the Secretariat, including regular reminders to missions of their responsibility to monitor real-time performance against the advance purchase policy using corporate dashboards and to investigate performance drivers and solutions. As noted in the most recent report of the Secretary-General on standards of accommodation for air travel (A/79/628), key performance drivers across the Secretariat are: late submission of travel requests; travel requests that were not “right the first time” and require rework, adding to the processing time; travel by “external” travellers such as meeting participants and external experts over whom the Secretariat has less administrative control; and circumstances outside the entities’ control such as travel document delays or operational issues, including emergencies or exigencies of service. Actions entities have taken to improve performance include: preparing and monitoring quarterly travel plans; escalating late travel requests to senior leadership within the entity; and regularly communicating to staff the process to comply with the policy.
Mine action activities

In 2025, the Mine Action Service continued to support special political missions with a mine action component by providing assistance in planning, programme design, implementation, reporting, and representation.

In the field, mine action efforts contributed to mandate delivery primarily through the provision of technical advice and expertise to mission leadership and relevant national counterparts. Specifically, in UNAMA, the mine action component provided explosive ordnance threat assessments, advised and coordinated mitigation measures in support of humanitarian and development initiatives, including support to the Mine Action Technical Cell, which leads nationwide coordination, quality assurance, and management of data on hazardous area to keep the United Nations, partners, and the public informed of the explosive threat. In accordance with its mandate of as contained in resolution 2626 (2022) and reaffirmed by subsequent resolutions, UNAMA supports existing mechanisms to improve the overall security situation in Afghanistan, provide assessments of the explosive ordnance threat and its impact on civilians, including children, advise and coordinate explosive ordnance threat mitigation measures in support of humanitarian and development initiatives, support the coordination of the humanitarian mine action sector. As the UNAMA’s current mine action capacity is not sufficient to undertake mine action coordination at the national level, the ability of UNAMA to undertake its  mine action mandate depends on a functioning Mine Action Technical Cell. Amid declining funding for the sector alongside a growing reliance on the coordination and data function, UNAMA plans to provide direct support to sustain the Mine Action Technical Cell core functions in 2027.

In UNSMIL, efforts focused on capacity building of the Libyan Mine Action Centre and relevant national security institutions in explosive ordnance clearance and weapons and ammunition management. Mine action also supported ceasefire implementation through engagement with the 5+5 Joint Military Commission and military demining teams from both the west and east.

In UNMHA, prior to 2025, mine action  efforts  centered on technical guidance to improve coordination among local authorities and with international partners. Following UNMHA’s closure pursuant to Security Council resolution 2813 (2026), technical guidance on mine action and coordination support in Yemen will continue under the auspices of Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen.
Ratios for vehicles and information technology equipment

In its resolution 80/243 A, the General Assembly endorsed the recommendation of the Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions for special political missions to limit, to the extent possible, the acquisition of new vehicles and laptops pending a review of the composition of their ground fleets and laptop holdings in the context of reduced operational footprints (A/80/7/Add.10, para. 65).  The missions continue to monitor excess holdings of vehicles and plan to dispose of vehicles once they meet established criteria, including life expectancy or write-off thresholds, or to recommend their transfer to other missions where feasible and cost-effective.

In the above context, the holdings of vehicles and information technology equipment are proposed on the basis of the anticipated personnel incumbency levels planned for 2027, as opposed to the full authorized level of personnel.
