Similarly, the guidelines issued by the Office of Information and Communications Technology (OICT) reinforced the “one computing device per user” policy as a best-practice reference to improve budget discipline, cost-effectiveness and alignment with Secretariat-wide ICT governance. Individual missions may deviate from the guidelines on the basis of operational requirements. Additionally, Missions have aligned their asset management practices with the updated lifecycle guidance issued by OICT, which extends the standard useful life of computing devices from four years to five-seven years. Decisions are based on assessments of security, operational, and performance considerations associated with operating devices beyond their traditional lifecycle. The total proposed computing device holdings for special political missions are 4.4 per cent higher than the standard allocation. Explanations for computing device holdings that are higher than the standard allocation in specific missions are as follows:

(a)	The computing device holdings at the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Syria are 12.7 per cent higher than the standard allocation, which is attributable to requirements for training purposes, security monitoring systems and servers;

(b)	The computing device holdings at the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen are 12.7 per cent higher than the standard allocation, which is attributable to requirements for training purposes, conference and meeting rooms, and servers;

(c)	The computing device holdings at UNOWAS are 14.5 per cent higher than the standard allocation, which is attributable to additional holdings required to provide for training purposes, conference and meeting rooms, data transmission and connectivity and servers and the CarLog system;

(d)	The computing device holdings for United Nations support for the Cameroon-Nigeria Mixed Commission are 211.8 per cent or two computers higher than the standard allocation, which is attributable to additional holdings required to provide for training and meeting rooms;
(e)	The computing device holdings for UNOCA are 3.7 per cent or 2 computers higher than the standard allocation, which is attributable to requirements for servers;

(f)	The computing device holdings for UNSMIL are 11.2 per cent higher than the standard allocation, which is attributable to requirements for training, the CarLog system, data transmission and connectivity and servers;

(g)	The computing device holdings at the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia are 3.6 per cent higher than the standard allocation, which is attributable to requirements for training purposes, Internet booths, data transmission and connectivity and servers;
(h)	The computing device holdings at BINUH are 6.9 per cent higher than the standard allocation, which is attributable to requirements for training purposes and servers;

(i)	The computing device holdings at UNAMA are 2.4 per cent higher than the standard allocation, which is attributable to additional holdings required to provide for training purposes, the CarLog system and servers, as well as provision for other personnel, including contractors.

The holdings are influenced by factors such as the need to provide for consultants and individual contractors, training facilities, Internet booths, information technology maintenance services, CarLog systems, programming of radios and fieldwork. Furthermore, based on the lessons learned during the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic, which saw a substantial increase in the use of virtual communications and remote working, it is critical to ensure the reliability of information technology equipment and infrastructure and their accessibility to all personnel, both staff and non-staff, to enable business continuity, mandate delivery and the safety and security of staff members, especially in the harsh environments where many special political missions operate.

The effective governance of information and communications technology (ICT) assets is a critical enabler of the Secretariat’s ability to deliver mandates efficiently, transparently and sustainably. OICT is advancing a Secretariat wide initiative to strengthen the integrity of ICT asset data recorded in Umoja, with the support of UNLB, Property Management and Inventory Control Unit of DOS and Global Asset Management Policy Service of the Field Operations Finance Division, DMSPC. This initiative is aligned with the ICT Strategy and is designed to support enterprise level visibility and oversight, while fully respecting the continued accountability of individual entities under the Delegation of Authority framework (ST/SGB/2019/2).

To this end, OICT is implementing a Global ICT Asset Management Project from 2026 to 2027. The objectives of this initiative are to: (a) establish an ICT Asset Lifecycle Management standard operating procedure (SOP) to harmonize how ICT assets are effectively managed across the Secretariat, leveraging on existing SOPs, guidance and practices already in place; (b) establish a reliable and authoritative dashboard in Umoja Analytics that provides visibility of ICT assets at both the enterprise and the entity levels; (c) improve the accuracy, completeness and integrity of ICT asset data in Umoja through data cleansing and validation; (e) enable analytical insights that support senior management and entity level decision making to support medium  and long term ICT planning; and (f) strengthen data governance and accountability related to ICT assets.
IV.		Budget formulation and management of resources
1.	Strengthening a culture of efficiency

The Secretariat continues to build on its strategic approach to developing and strengthening its culture of efficiency, launched in January 2025 at a Secretary-General’s seminar with all Special Representatives of the Secretary-General of peacekeeping and special political missions as well as Personal and Special Envoys of the Secretary-General. The theme of a culture of efficiency was once again on the agenda at the 2026 meeting, which stressed the importance of leadership in deepening the culture of efficiency at both the organizational and individual staff levels, especially in light of the particularly difficult financial environment for the Organization. The Field Operations Finance Division in the Department of Management Strategy, Policy and Compliance is collaborating with the Leadership Support Section of the Departments of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs and Peace Operations to plan further support to the Special Representatives of the Secretary-General of peacekeeping and special political missions to strengthen implementation of this culture of efficiency in the field, including by conducting webinars with mission senior leaders and sharing best practices across missions.

To support the strategic approach across missions, the Field Operations Finance Division has also: (a) organized global briefings and individual workshops with missions to guide them through the efficiency methodology; (b) collate each mission’s main efficiency initiatives into an aide-memoire to inspire and inform efforts across missions; (c) developed standardized templates for missions to calculate efficiencies, including one-time efficiency initiatives, initiatives requiring upfront investments, and related break-even points. Missions have been encouraged to continue reflecting and reporting on these and to consider adding or expanding others. This includes considering repurposing vacant or long vacant posts with the same mandate delivery or output. Missions were also requested to identify cost avoidance and cost reductions, which will involve taking proactive action to avoid future expenses, such as the inter-mission transfer of assets.

In quantifiable terms, enhancements in budgeting policy and efficiency initiatives resulted in actual savings of $16.8 million in 2025 for special political missions as compared to the $9.3 million projected. Similarly, the projected quantifiable savings and costs avoided amount to approximately $14.7 million for 2027, representing 3.6 per cent of the 2026 appropriation for the continuing missions. This represents sustainable savings for the Organization.
The major management improvements and efficiency measures applied and efforts to achieve sustained cost reductions and cost avoidance are reflected in the following areas:

civilian personnel, resulting from (i) the proposed abolishment of 61 posts and the downward reclassification of two posts (1 P‑5 and 1 P‑4) in UNAMA, reflecting targeted efficiency measures through organizational optimization, functional streamlining and improved resource allocation, (ii) the reduction of high level posts (D-1 and above), comprising the abolishment of 1 USG in Support to the implementation of Security Council resolution 1559 (2004), 1 D-1 in the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia and 1 D-1 in BINUH, and the downward reclassification  of 1 D-1 post to the P-5 level in the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Syria, (iii)); the nationalization of two international posts (1 P‑3 and 1 P‑2) to National Professional Officers in the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia, and (iv) the promotion of national capacity for the delivery of critical mandated activities in UNSMIL;

air operations, reflecting the discontinuation of the rental and operation of fixed‑wing aircraft and the consolidation of aviation requirements in the United Nations Verification Mission in Colombia; the establishment of a cost‑recovery arrangement for the use of air assets of the United Nations Support Office in Haiti (UNSOH) in lieu of a separate aviation contract in BINUH; and the use of commercial airlines in UNOCA in lieu of the use of special flights associated with its cost-shared fixed wing aircraft;
facilities and infrastructure, reflecting reduced fuel consumption for generators resulting from project upgrades in UNAMA and fuel‑optimization measures in UNSCOL; and
cost avoidance related to the non-acquisition of vehicles, equipment or supplies owing to the transfer of assets from UNIFIL in UNSCOL.
Further details of the efficiency measures achieved by mission are provided in the proposed budget reports of the respective thematic clusters.

Most missions are also reducing the proposed resources for official travel and are instead encouraging the use of virtual meetings where feasible, optimizing travel schedules, coordinating with partners to maximize impact while minimizing costs and prioritizing the use of online training options’ and the budgets also reflect economies of scale vis-à-vis the provision of materials and services and substantive support as part of mandated activities in the context of various cost-sharing arrangements.
2.	Improved budgeting methodologies

Within the framework of the Secretary-General’s UN80 Initiative, missions were requested to explore opportunities  to recalibrate their operations with a view to delivering mandates efficiently with reduced resources, while maintaining due regard for the security and safety of personnel and facilities. Maintaining the momentum, the formulation of the 2027 budget proposals emphasized enhanced discipline and accountability, supported by data-driven analysis.  In this context, the following principles were applied:

Enhancing the overall effectiveness by accommodating, where appropriate, the resource implications of new and expanded mandates within existing resources, with additional costs offset through efficiency gains, reprioritization or redeployment of existing resources;

Applying a data-driven approach to budget formulation, taking into account operational necessity, actual utilization and implementation capacity,  in the context of the current financial situation. This included analysis of the cancellation of prior period commitments and, where appropriate, the application of zero-based budgeting to reduce reliance on historic budget levels;

Adopting a multi-year perspective for construction planning and oversight of major capital projects, as well as a multi-year approach for asset management as a core component of mission budget planning, particularly with respect to air assets, and replacement planning for vehicles and information and communications technology projects; and

Prioritizing the use of existing assets, including the United Nations Reserve, strategic deployment stocks (SDS), the return, refurbishment and reuse programme (3R), and identified surplus property from other entities, prior to proposing the procurement of new items.

With respect to air operations, missions were requested to review carefully their requirements for air assets and to maximize opportunities for the sharing of air assets across missions, with support from the Department of Operational Support. The 2027 budgetary proposals reflect requirements for air assets that are assessed as necessary and well-utilized air assets. Budgeting for flight hours continues to be guided by the aviation budgeting policy introduced in 2025 and informed by the latest utilization data.

To strengthen oversight of ICT projects and activities and related resource requirements, the budget proposals from the special political missions were subject to review and technical clearance by the Office of Information and Communications Technology. The process is intended to support strategic planning, align demand plans with budget proposals and implementation capacity, avoid duplication of efforts and promote efficiency gains.

To ensure consistency and coherence, the proposed post actions adhere consistently to definitions pertaining to changes in staffing, and the proposals are fully justified in terms of changes in mandates or operational circumstances and workload requirements.

In addition, the Secretariat has ensured that all general temporary assistance positions are fully justified under each mission, providing the reasons for their proposed retention in 2027. In addition, no proposals have been made to convert these positions to regular posts. Should future assessment lead to a determination that such capacities should be regularized, proper proposals will be made in future budgets.
3.	Consistent application of the latest standard rates

With regard to international staff costs in field locations, the budgetary rates for net salary and staff assessment for 2027 were determined for each grade level and for each special political mission according to the following methodology:

(a)	With regard to international staff, the most recent salary scale, effective 1 January 2026, as approved by the General Assembly in its resolution 80/236, was used for net salary and staff assessment for each level in the Professional and higher categories. Similarly, the net base salary scale for staff in the Field Service category is adjusted, effective 1 January 2026 (in accordance with standing practice in line with the ICSC decision contained in A/45/30, para. 270 (e));
(b)	The step levels selected for each grade are based on the actual average step levels for each mission as at 31 December 2025, using actual incumbency data for international staff;
(c)	The post adjustment multiplier for each duty station as of April 2026 was applied to the net base salary rates.

With regard to national staff, the most recent salary scales as of April 2026 were used for net salary and staff assessment, with common staff costs as a percentage of net salaries, based on actual expenditure for the period from 1 January to 31 December 2025, applied to the average grade and step of national staff.

With regard to common staff costs, the actual expenditure from 1 January to 31 December 2025 was used to calculate common staff costs as a percentage of net salaries (inclusive of post adjustment but net of staff assessment) to determine the percentage of common staff costs for 2027. However, considering the significant and exceptional expenditures related to separation costs in the context of the two early separation programmes in 2025, actual expenditures for the period were adjusted to exclude one-time separation costs arising from the early separation programme exercises. A multi-year comparative analysis and a more detailed analysis by commitment item was used for each mission to determine if there were any other substantive or operational reasons for any significant changes.

With regard to danger pay, the proposed requirements reflect the discontinuation of danger pay, effective 1 April 2026, for all areas and duty station in Syria, and Benghazi and Sirte in Libya, as in line with the latest updates from the International Civil Service Commission (ICSC).

For United Nations Headquarters, offices away from Headquarters and the regional commission duty stations (New York, Geneva, Nairobi, Addis Ababa, Bangkok and Beirut), the standard costs for salaries and common staff costs for the programme budget were used.

With regard to military contingents (United Nations Guard Units), the latest single rate of reimbursement to countries contributing contingent personnel to United Nations field operations in the amount of $1,448 per person per month effective 1 July 2022, and the recreation leave allowance of $11.50 per day for up to 15 days of leave taken during each six-month period, as approved by the General Assembly in its resolutions 76/274 and 76/276, were applied. Reimbursement related to contingent-owned equipment is based on the rates adopted by the Assembly in its resolution 77/303. In this regard, the recommendations of the 2026 Working Group on Contingent-Owned Equipment (A/80/636) are currently under consideration by the General Assembly. Should the Assembly approve the recommended net average increase of 1.58 per cent in the wet lease rates for major equipment and the reimbursement rates for self-sustainment proposed to take effect on 1 July 2026, the related additional financial implications have not been included in the present budget proposal.

With regard to military advisers, observers, United Nations police and government-provided personnel, the latest applicable mission subsistence allowance rates for each country and mission area effective from 1 January 2026 were applied, as per the rates promulgated by the Office of Human Resources in December 2025.

With regard to experts, the estimates considered the latest fee ranges issued by the Office of Human Resources. The cost-of-living allowance for non-home-based experts in the Security Council sanctions committee panels and other support mechanisms, the latest monthly rates of $6,600 (New York) as approved by the Office of Human Resources, which took effect from 1 March 2023, have been applied to the five missions that have such requirements.

With regard to rental of premises in New York, the latest unit rate of $15,000 per person per year, effective 1 January 2025, has been applied to those missions accommodated on the Headquarters premises in New York.

With respect to fuel costs, the average price per litre for the different types of fuel in the six-month period from October 2025 to March 2026 have been used as the basis for calculating the provisions for fuel costs under the respective budget classes for 2027.
For ICT, the budget proposals also reflect the latest standard rates and service charges issued by the Office of Information and Communications Technology.
4.	Standardized methodology of budgeted vacancy rates

The Field Operations Finance Division provided guidance to all special political missions to improve the accuracy and consistency of the vacancy rate factors applied in the proposed budgets for 2027, to ensure that the proposed vacancy rates are based, as much as possible, on actual rates.

The proposed vacancy rates applied in the budget for 2027, for all types of personnel, have taken into account the experience to date. The assumptions considered for the proposed vacancy rates include: (a) the 12-month average vacancy rate from January to December in 2025; and (b) the actual vacancy rate as at 31 March 2026. The lower of the two was used as the budgeted vacancy rate.  For missions with a high number of abolitions included in the proposed 2027 budget, namely BINUH and UNAMA, the proposed vacancy rates for civilian personnel categories with abolishments were estimated using the total number of vacant posts and positions as of 31 March 2026 (exclusive of posts approved for phased abolishment in 2026), net of the number of posts and positions proposed for abolition. For the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen, the proposed vacancy rates reflect their planned deployment during the period, following the closure of UNMHA. This is in line with the policy guidance to improve the accuracy and consistency of the vacancy factors applied in the proposed budgets for 2027 and to ensure that the proposed vacancy rates are based, as much as possible, on actual rates.

For proposed establishment of new posts or positions, or posts or positions proposed for reassignment, a vacancy rate of 50 per cent has been applied in the calculation of costs of such posts. In addition, a vacancy rate of 50 per cent has been used for posts proposed for conversion.

In addition, all special political missions were requested to take into full consideration the recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions and requests from the General Assembly that vacant posts and positions should be filled expeditiously. While efforts continue to fill vacant posts as expeditiously as possible, the current liquidity situation also requires careful planning of recruitment and onboarding to minimize the financial impacts.

The Field Operations Finance Division provided guidance to all special political missions to take the opportunity offered during the preparation of the 2027 budget to critically review long-vacant posts with a view to abolishing vacant posts that can be covered by existing capacities, or to propose reassignment or abolishment with the aim of facilitating the establishment of another function to address a more critical need, or to propose conversion to a national post.

Information on all posts vacant for more than two years and posts encumbered through special post allowances for more than one year is included in the supplementary information under each thematic cluster, which details the vacancy or special post allowance start dates, level and functional title of the posts, organizational unit and current status of recruitment, and provides justification for the retention of long-vacant posts.
5. 	Harmonization of budget presentation of cluster III missions

In line with the recommendation of the ACABQ as contained in A/59/569/Add.1, para. 6, that the Secretary-General should consider ways and means to present the budgets of large missions in a manner that would be more suitable for their size and complexity, the Secretariat has reassessed the optimum ways to present the budget requirements for UNAMA, in view of the evolution of mandates and resources over the last two decades. Given that UNAMA thematically belongs to cluster III, and its shares many similar characteristics with similarly-sized field missions under cluster III, the Secretary-General considers that integrating UNAMA into the report on thematic cluster III offers a more harmonized structure and presentation across missions of similar magnitude and size. This also leads to efficiencies in report production as well as reviews by the legislative bodies, in line with the objectives of the UN80 initiative.
At the same time, the presentation of cluster III has been further enhanced through the inclusion of addition tables, annexes and narratives. The key benefits of the adjustments include:

Greater consistency: A harmonized structure and presentation across UNAMA and the other missions within thematic cluster III is expected to enhance clarity and improve comparability of information for Member States, the Advisory Committee, oversight bodies and the Secretariat, thereby supporting more efficient analysis and review.

Fewer but higher-quality reports: A reduced number of reports, from five to four, and the corresponding outputs of the Advisory Committee is expected to streamline deliberations and ease the documentation burden for legislative bodies, including the Fifth Committee. It is further expected to enhance readability and generate savings in editorial, translation and text-processing costs.

Maintained analytical depth: Detailed mission-specific budget information will continue to be provided to ensure full visibility of resource requirements and support informed oversight. In this regard, more focused and analytical information is presented in tabular format in both the fascicles and the supplementary information, including -summary views of and detailed data on all post actions by mission, as well as expanded financial information by class of expenditure.
6.	Improved presentation of financial performance

In response to the recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions (see A/80/7/Add.10, para. 70 and A/80/7/Add.1 para. 29) and endorsed by the General Assembly in it resolution 80/243 A, the Secretariat is continuing its efforts to enhance the financial performance reporting of the special political missions in the context of the present report, the financial performance report of the programme budget and the supplementary information provided for the special political missions. To this end, more comprehensive and detailed information on the financial performance is being provided. For supplementary information, analyses of variances for the performance and the proposed budget period are presented together in all relevant tables and sections. Information and justifications for unliquidated obligations and the cancellation of prior-period obligations is provided in table 6 and paragraphs 144 and 145 below, with further detailed information included in the financial performance report on the programme budget for 2025 (A/81/89) and the supplementary information.  In addition, for air operations, mine actions and construction projects for field-based special political missions under thematic cluster III, information has been included in the supplementary information for those missions, as is done for peacekeeping operations, in response to the recommendations of the Advisory Committee (see A/78/7/Add.1, para. 56).

Additional information on the evolution of financial resources by mission over the most recent five years is provided in table 11 of the present report. Additional information on the evolution of financial resources for each mission, broken down by budget class, over that period, including both appropriation and expenditure, is provided in the supplementary information for each thematic cluster, similar to the rest of the regular budget, in response to the recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions (see A/78/7, para. 7).

children.text: Variance analysis –  – Overall
The General Assembly in its resolutions 80/243 A and 79/254 approved resources in the amount of $536.1 million for special political missions for 2026.

The vacancy rates for 2026 were those included in the initial proposed programme budget and were not updated in the context of the revised estimates, as a result of the reduction in the number of posts and positions proposed for 2026. The magnitude of changes proposed, which included a combination of both vacant and encumbered posts, the impact of the ongoing recruitment freeze, the early separation programme exercises made it challenging to present updated proposed vacancy rates as part of the revised estimates proposal within the expected timeframes for the submission of the report.

As special political missions were not part of the recosting exercise carried out for the regular budget, the lack of update to the vacancy rates means that the 2026 appropriation was under-budgeted by $19.3 million, which was noted by the Advisory Committee in its report (A/80/7/Add.10, para. 26). This amount includes an estimated increase of $11.4 million for continuing missions (excluding UNTMIS and UNMHA), which had to be absorbed within the approved 2026 budget.

For 2027, the proposed budget amounts to $419.4 million, representing an increase of $7.1 million or 1.7 per cent, compared to the approved budget for 2026 for these continuing missions. Within this context, the special political missions are proposing to absorb $4.3 million of the estimated additional requirements of $11.4 million referred to in paragraph 123 above, through efficiency measures, reprioritization and the redeployment of existing post and non-post resources.
Cluster I

The proposed resource requirements for the 12 missions under thematic cluster I for 2027 amount to $56.3 million, representing a net increase of $5.0 million (9.7 per cent) compared with 2026. The overall increase is attributable primarily to: (a) increased requirements under civilian personnel, owing to the application of lower vacancy rates and revised salary rates; and (b) increased operational costs, mainly due to the provisioning of a full year in 2027, compared to nine months budgeted in 2026, of requirements under air operations for the rental and operation of one fixed-wing aircraft, and under facilities and infrastructure for the rental of premises and security services, for the Office of the Special Envoy for Yemen following the transfer as of 1 April 2026 of residual tasks previously performed by the United Nations Mission to Support the Hudaydah Agreement (UNMHA) pursuant to Security Council resolution 2813 (2026). The increase was offset in part by: (a) reduced requirements under communications and information technology, owing to lower needs for the acquisition of equipment and reduced subscription costs for periodicals and publications; and (b) reduced requirements underground transportation, owing to lower needs for rental of vehicles and spare parts.
Cluster II

The proposed resource requirements for the 15 continuing missions under thematic cluster II for 2027 amount to $37.7 million, representing a net increase of $1.3 million (3.6 per cent) compared with 2026. The overall increase is attributable primarily to: (a) increased requirements for civilian personnel resulting from the application of lower vacancy rates and the application of the latest salary rates; and (b) increased requirements for expert fees, reflecting changes in the budgeted average monthly fees based on the current composition of expert teams. The increase was offset in part by: (a) lower estimated common staff costs for national staff, based on actual past expenditures related staff entitlements; and (b) reduced requirements for communications and information technology, reflecting the non-recurrent provision for the acquisition of equipment included in the 2026 approved budget, as well as lower requirements for subscriptions to specialized databases and news resources to support and supplement investigations and research.
Cluster III

The proposed resource requirements for the nine continuing missions under thematic cluster III amount to $325.4 million, representing a net increase of $0.8 million f (0.2 per cent) compared with 2026. The overall increase is attributable primarily to increased requirements for civilian personnel resulting from the application of lower vacancy rates and the application of the latest salary rates. The increase was offset in part by reduced requirements: (a) resulting from the proposed net abolishment of 89 posts and positions, especially in UNAMA and BINUH; (b) the reduction of the BINUH’s footprint due to the handover of support functions to UNSOH and the downsizing of the mandate; (c) reduced rental and maintenance costs for the  premises in Tripoli based on latest contractual arrangement, as well as well as exclusion of a non-recurrent provision for security construction approved in 2026 in UNSMIL; (d) reduced requirements under air operations owing to the downsizing of the mission’s fleet by two aircraft in UN Verification Mission in Colombia, and a reduction in flight hours based on the latest utilization rates in UNSMIL and UNAMA; (e) lower communication carrier and connectivity costs, as well as reduced centralized services costs, resulting from efficiency measures taken since 2025 that included the lower staffing levels and the closure of 10 sub-regional offices in the UN Verification Mission in Colombia;  (f) reduced requirements for fuel for generators reflecting energy-efficiency measures and a reduced mission footprint following the closure and nationalization of field offices approved in 2026 in UNAMA; and (g) reduced requirements for military and police personnel resulting from the reconfiguration of deployments in UNSMIL and BINUH.
Share of the cost of the Regional Service Centre in Entebbe

The special political missions’ share of the cost of RSCE reflects an increase of $0.9 million, attributable mainly to an increase of the share of special political missions in the cost of the Centre, from 5.10 per cent in the 2025/26 period to 7.17 per cent in the 2026/27 period. This reflects the expanded client base of the Centre, following the integration of former clients of KJSO of which seven are continuing special political missions.

children.text: Contribution of extrabudgetary resources to mandate implementation in special political missions

Extrabudgetary resources, in particular voluntary contributions, continue to be used for bolstering backstopping, surge requirements for good offices, crisis situations and other activities related to the mandates of special political missions. Such resources have also been critical for support for inter-mission activities and for visits by desk officers and senior officials to missions.

Voluntary contributions have been important in enabling special political missions to implement targeted projects in pursuit of the implementation of their mandates. In the Great Lakes region, the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General utilizes extrabudgetary resources to support the implementation of the project for the reduction of small arms circulation in the Great Lakes region. The Office of the Special Adviser to the Secretary-General on the Prevention of Genocide utilizes extrabudgetary resources to support the capacity-building and technical assistance programme and the preparation of the 2026 report of the Secretary-General on the responsibility to protect. The Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen continues to utilize extrabudgetary resources to support the Special Envoy’s efforts to reach sustainable and inclusive agreements to end the conflict in country.  The Office of the Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for the Sudan utilizes extrabudgetary resources to support the provision of critical expertise on security arrangements and ceasefires, as well as support for communication strategies and media engagement for the Personal Envoy. UNSMIL continues to utilize extrabudgetary resources to support activities focused on facilitating an inclusive intra-Libyan political process, an economic track and capacity-building on human rights. UNAMA utilizes extrabudgetary resources to support; climate change, activities in local peace initiatives and political engagement and meetings with regional governments, and the advancement of international engagement on Afghanistan in a more coherent, coordinated, and structured manner in line with the recommendations of the Independent Assessment on Afghanistan (S/2023/856).

In addition, voluntary contributions fund specific mission initiatives. The mission in support of the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1540 (2004) on the non-proliferation of all weapons of mass destruction to non-State actors used extrabudgetary resources in 2025 to support the participation of Member States in activities aimed at advancing the implementation of the resolution, including capacity- building and outreach initiatives. Furthermore, the Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directorate utilizes extrabudgetary resources to support the implementation of Committee-mandated activities and relevant projects, including the organization of meetings in line with the Committee’s approved programme of work and the promotion of international cooperation in counter-terrorism. This includes targeted capacity-building initiatives, such as projects aimed at strengthening national capabilities to detect and disrupt terrorist activities, including through the use of information and communications technologies, as well as specialized initiatives on forensics and biometrics in Africa.

Voluntary contributions also bolster backstopping capacity at Headquarters, including by funding regular visits to the field, thereby enabling the development of closer collaboration with missions. Such visits have facilitated a better understanding and analysis of the context in which missions are operating and how they can be better supported to implement their mandates.

In addition, cost-recovery revenue in some missions, such as UNAMA, enabled them to provide shared common services to other agencies, funds and programmes in the same location, to benefit from economies of scale. This is in line with the direction of consolidating support services at country level and the requirement for integrated support across the United Nations system for the 2030 Agenda. Cost recovery is governed by rule 105.11 of the Financial Regulations and Rules of the United Nations, in addition to policy guidance issued by the Controller.

Extrabudgetary resources (including both voluntary contributions and cost-recovery revenue) are estimated at $33.0 million for 2027, compared with an estimated $33.3 million in 2026. The projected decrease of $0.3 million for 2027 is attributable to the anticipated conclusion or non-extension of some projects or activities in the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General on Myanmar, United Nations support for the Cameroon-Nigeria Mixed Commission and UNAMA, offset by increases in contributions in Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for the Great Lakes Region and Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen, based on current projections. Extrabudgetary resources have been important in enabling special political missions to implement targeted projects in pursuit of their mandates. However, while missions continue to engage actively in fundraising activities, it remains a challenge to secure funding or pledges for 2027 sufficiently in advance to enable projections to be made with greater certainty.
Human resources

The number of civilian personnel proposed for 2027, including international and national staff, United National Volunteers and general temporary assistance positions, reflects an overall decrease of 89 posts and positions, from 2,393 to 2,304. Details of the human resources requirements by cluster, by mission and by category of personnel are presented in tables 13 to 16.
Backstopping support at Headquarters

Special political missions rely on Headquarters for backstopping support for a wide range of functions. The Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs is leading and providing substantive backstopping to 34 of the 36 continuing special political missions by ensuring regular and effective communication between the missions and United Nations entities in New York and regular liaison with Member States through their permanent missions to the United Nations and preparing a wide range of substantive material, including briefing material for the Security Council and regular reports of the Secretary-General, among other functions. Administrative support is being provided by the one-Executive-Office of DOS.

Special political missions also benefit from operational support and advisory services in the areas of human resources and supply chain management provided by DOS; budgetary and financial services, asset and property management policy support and assistance with accountability systems provided by DMSPC; and information technology support delivered by the OICT. Special political missions also rely on support from Headquarters in thematic and operational areas such as constitution-making, electoral assistance, mediation, best practices, military and police planning/force generation, rule of law and security institutions.

As outlined in detail in the report of the Secretary-General on the review of arrangements for funding and backstopping special political missions (A/66/340), which remained pending before the General Assembly, there is no dedicated mechanism to ensure relevant capacities for backstopping special political missions at Headquarters, in contrast to peacekeeping operations, which can draw on the support account for peacekeeping operations.

In 2026, a total of 36 posts (1 D-1, 8 P-5, 18 P-4, 3 P-3, and 6 General Service (Other level)) are being funded from special political missions. In 2027, a total of 30 such posts (1 D-1, 7 P-5, 14 P-4, 2 P-3 and 6 General Service (Other level)) are proposed, reflecting the abolishment of 6 posts in 2026 due to the mandate termination, comprising of 2 posts (1 P-4 and 1 P-3), effective 31 March 2026, funded from UNMHA, and 4 posts (1 P-5, and 3 P-4) funded from UNTMIS.

While the resources included in the budgets of special political missions for backstopping support are fundamental for the Secretariat to provide support to special political missions, the regular budget and extra budgetary resources of the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs are often also required to ensure adequate support. Similarly, the regular budget and extrabudgetary resources of the Office for Disarmament Affairs are used to provide administrative support to the mission in support of the Security Council Committee established pursuant to resolution 1540 (2004) on the non-proliferation of all weapons of mass destruction.

Financial performance of special political missions for 2025

The General Assembly approved an overall appropriation for 2025 of $693.0 million for the special political missions (resolutions 79/258 A and 79/258 B). The expenditure for 2025 amounted to $632.4 million, resulting in an overall unencumbered balance of $60.6 million, or 8.7 per cent. The overall implementation rate of 91.3 remains consistent with the previous year (92 per cent in 2024) owing to continued spending restrictions imposed due to the liquidity constraints and the efforts to curtail expenditure across special political missions. An analysis of the main factors affecting budget performance is provided in table 17. Performance reporting has been enhanced through the inclusion of information for field-based missions in the financial performance report on the programme budget for 2025 (A/81/89), in line with the recommendation of the Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions (see A/79/7/Add.1, para. 10). A.	Terminology related to proposed changes in human resources
1.	The following terms have been applied with respect to proposed changes in human resources:

•	Post establishment: a new post is proposed to be established when additional resources are necessary and when it is not possible to redeploy resources from other offices or otherwise accommodate specific activities from within existing resources.

•	Post reassignment: an approved post that was intended to cover a certain function is proposed to implement other priority mandated activities unrelated to the original function. While a post reassignment may involve a change of location or office, it does not change the category or level of the post.
•	Post redeployment: an approved post is proposed to be redeployed to cover comparable or related functions in another office.
•	Post reclassification: an approved post is proposed to be reclassified (upgraded or downgraded) when the duties and responsibilities of the post have changed substantially.

•	Post abolishment: an approved post is proposed to be abolished if it is no longer needed to implement the activities for which it was approved or to implement other priority mandated activities within the mission.
•	Post conversion: three possible options for post conversion are as follows:

–	Conversion of general temporary assistance positions to posts: approved positions financed under general temporary assistance are proposed for conversion to posts if the functions being performed are of a continuing nature.
–	Conversion of international staff posts to national staff posts: approved international staff posts are proposed for conversion to national staff posts.

–	Conversion of the approved source of funding: positions funded under extrabudgetary resources are proposed for conversion to be funded under the regular budget. Other attributes of the positions would remain unchanged.
B.	Terminology related to variance analysis
2.	The contributing factors for the resource variance according to specific standard options encompass the following categories listed below:
•	New and expanded mandates: variances caused by changes in the scale or scope of the mandate.

•	Technical adjustments: variances caused by adjustments due to increased provisions for posts approved for the preceding budget proposals with a 50 per cent vacancy rate that are subject to the proposed vacancy rate for continuing posts in the current proposed budget period. Other adjustments of a technical nature include changes in salary rates, vacancy rates, contractual rates or other changes in cost parameters as a result of United Nations regulations, rules and policies.
•	Other changes: variances caused by resource changes that do not fall under the above factors.

Action taken to implement the recommendation or request
Resolution 80/243

Stresses that the UN80 Initiative is not a liquidity management measure, and requires going beyond a one-time reform exercise to also incorporate a culture of efficiency to ensure long-term effective and efficient mandate delivery, affirms the respective roles of the General Assembly and the Security Council with regard to special political missions, and requests the Secretary-General to pursue synergies to achieve greater efficiency in the management of post and non‑post resources, and to this end present proposals in his next budget submissions, while taking into account the different sizes, complexities and operational environments of special political missions (sect. XVII, para. 4).
Information on the efforts of the Secretariat to pursue synergies is detailed under the section on building and strengthening a culture of efficiency, paragraphs 88 to 93.

Recognizes the need to assess the impact of the reform efforts on mandate implementation, requests the Secretary-General to reflect thereon in his future budget submissions for special political missions, and also requests the Secretary-General to explore measures to apply zero-based budgeting, based on mandated activities (sect. XVII, para. 5).

Where applicable, the proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects changes arising from the UN80 Initiative. In particular, the tables of deliverables for each mission reflect updated planned deliverables for 2026, in line with the approved programme budget for 2026. Such changes, as applicable, are articulated in the respective thematic cluster report. 
Information on improved budgeting methodologies, including the continued application of zero-based budgeting is detailed in paragraph 95 of the present report.

children.text: B.	Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions

table_content.text: Brief description of the recommendation or request
Action taken to implement the recommendation or request
Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions (A/80/7/Add.10), as endorsed by the General Assembly in its resolution 80/243 A

The Advisory Committee notes that there are 3 posts proposed for conversion from international to national posts (including 2 National Professional Officer) and 11 national posts proposed for establishment for 2026. The Committee notes, however, that eight of the new posts proposed for establishment are proposed in conjunction with the proposed abolishment of eight national posts (see A/80/7/Add.14, paras. 21 and 25). The Committee notes with concern that the revised estimates contain only a limited number of proposals aimed at nationalization and the creation of national posts. The Committee is of the view that the current proposals do not take advantage of the review exercise to enhance national capacity development while adopting cost effective measures. The Committee trusts that a more strategic approach, including the identification of functions conducive to nationalization, will guide continuing efforts in the context of the UN80 Initiative and beyond and that information in that regard will be presented in future budget reports.  (para. 32).

As part of the budget formulation process, missions were required to consider options for greater nationalization of functions, commensurate with mandate requirements and operational needs.  The section on promoting national capacities (paras. 60- 63) contains information on the continued efforts by the special political missions to promote the nationalization of posts in response to the recommendation of the Advisory Committee.

The Advisory Committee has acknowledged the efforts made by the Secretariat to achieve cost efficiency, including by strengthening a data-driven approach in formulating budgetary requirements for air operations for special political missions. The Committee notes the measures undertaken to seek efficiencies and enhance the utilization of air fleets by maximizing opportunities for the sharing of air assets across missions and a portfolio of standby air solutions. The Committee trusts that efforts will be continued to ensure that the air fleets in the missions are used in the most effective and efficient manner, such as by exploring the possibility of refining the applied methodology to attribute greater weight to the latest utilization data, and that information in that regard will be provided in the next budget report. The Committee considers that there are possibilities for more cooperation among missions, in particular those located within the same proximity, with a view to ensuring the efficient and effective use of missions’ resources, as an important element of consolidation of the culture of efficiency in field operations, without prejudice to the implementation of mandates of individual missions. The Committee is also of the view that enhanced system-wide cooperation in the context of the UN80 Initiative presents an opportunity also to explore opportunities for further cooperation in the use of air assets, as appropriate. The Committee considers that Headquarters should provide guidance and proposals to missions on possible optimal arrangements of their air fleet and mechanisms for inter-mission cooperation with a view to promoting optimization and cost effectiveness of the use of resources (see A/79/724, paras. 41–42; and A/79/7/Add.1, para. 48) (para. 38).

The Secretariat has taken measures to seek efficiencies and enhance the utilization of the air fleets. 
The Secretariat continues to implement the category management strategy for commercial and military aviation, which is intended to improve aviation support efficiency and effectiveness, while meeting clients’ demands.
To increase the Secretariat’s agility and responsiveness, DOS has expanded its portfolio of air solutions. In addition to the long-term air charter agreements and military aircraft services under letters of assistance, DOS has increased options for air services to include standby charter agreements, air ambulance services, and aircraft services under letters of assistance.
Additionally, the Secretariat established the On-Call Logistics Capabilities Augmentation initiative in January 2025. The initiative enhances the United Nations’ ability to respond swiftly in emergencies by leveraging on-call support through pre-established arrangements with Member States. This includes critical resources such as aircraft for evacuation and delivery of supplies. In doing so, the initiative significantly boosts the United Nations’ surge capacity during crises and its ability to respond to ad hoc requests, thereby offering improved, efficient and timely support.
Missions continue to make efforts to ensure that their air operation requirements are fulfilled in the most effective and efficient manner, including through inter-mission cooperation with other special political missions or peacekeeping missions, when possible.
In UNOCA, the Office has reviewed its operational requirement for a dedicated aircraft in view of the non-utilization of the fixed wing during 2024 and 2025 owing to liquidity constraints and the high cost of special flights. In response, the Office has prioritized the use of commercial airlines for official travel during the preceding two financial periods and plans to continue this approach, resulting in the removal of the provision for air operations. 
UNAMA continues to explore the use of the regional on-call aircraft charter agreements such as those for the provision of air ambulance, aero-medical and aero-casualty evacuation services.  Further the mission uses a data-driven approach to plan its air fleet taskings and flight routing, aimed to optimize the use of its aircraft.  Under the established memorandum of understanding with the United Nations Humanitarian Air Service on cooperation in air operations, UNAMA uses their services when it is more cost-effective to transport its passengers and cargo with UNHAS aircraft rather than to task its dedicated aircraft.  Because of its geographic location, opportunities for inter-mission cooperation, including with peacekeeping missions remain limited. Such support would entail long and empty positioning and dispositioning flights. UNAMA therefore requires dedicated aircraft to be deployed to the Mission area of responsibility on a continuous basis.

The Advisory Committee considers that efforts should be intensified to maximize the use of virtual meetings and to combine travel, with a view to limiting costs strictly to the minimum necessary. The Committee trusts that further efficiencies under official travel will continue to be explored and presented in the proposed programme budget for 2027 (para. 39).

Missions continue to implement measures to minimize their requirements under official travel, including prioritizing the appropriate use of technology to attend virtual meetings and online training and minimizing travel requirements to attend workshops, conferences and meetings.
For the Panel of Experts, efficiency gains have been achieved for official travel of staff and expert travel requirements through the use of virtual meetings and the consolidation of travel itineraries, where feasible, as well as through the use of regional meeting formats with intelligence counterparts by the Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team.

The Advisory Committee, while noting the improvement made in the overall compliance rates during 2024, recalls that the General Assembly, in its resolution 77/263 B, reiterated its serious concern at the low compliance with the advance purchase policy directive in all travel categories and requested the Secretary-General to take more effective measures to improve the situation in order to reduce air travel costs, given that most official travel is not carried out for the purpose of emergency situations or unforeseen requirements (resolution 77/263 B, para. 8) (ibid.). (para. 41).

The overall performance for all special political missions has shown increases year on year from 18 per cent in 2019 to 50 per cent in 2025, reflecting  continued efforts by Missions to comply with the advance purchase policy and monitor closely compliance to ensure full adherence to policy requirements.  Such efforts include the strengthening of internal controls to ensured that official travel is planned sufficiently in advance to significantly reduce air travel costs, reduction of travel processing times, increased sensitization to staff members on compliance of the rule, enhanced monitoring of compliance enabled through timely follow up by travel focal points.

In its first report on the proposed programme budget for 2026 (A/80/7, chap. I, para. 69), the Advisory Committee recalled its recommendation endorsed by the General Assembly in its resolution 79/257 for the Secretary-General to make the arrangements necessary to track information on all expenditures corresponding to the appropriated amounts for training and to report thereon in future budget submissions and financial performance reports. The Committee notes that, while there have been adjustments in missions’ proposed resources for training in the context of the revised estimates for 2026, the per capita cost of training has increased in all missions, except UNAMI and the Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary General for the Horn of Africa (para. 44).
Information on training expenditures is provided in the supplementary information packages.

The Advisory Committee acknowledges the efforts undertaken to identify efficiencies in the budget proposal for 2026 for the special political missions and further efforts in the revised estimates in the context of the UN80 Initiative. The Committee underscores the need for sustainable and quantifiable efficiency measures and gains, with transparent methodology, and an enhanced culture of efficiency for the Organization. The Committee has highlighted efficiencies that go beyond organizational restructuring and be anchored in a rigorous, transparent methodology applied by all entities to ensure consistency and comparability of results and be grounded in systematic workload and performance analysis (A/80/7, chap. I, para. 13). para. 46).
Information on the efforts undertaken and planned to strengthen a culture of efficiency is detailed under the section on building and strengthening a culture of efficiency, paragraphs 88 to 93.

Without prejudice to the distinct mandates of each entity, and subject to the decisions of the legislative bodies, as appropriate, the Advisory Committee trusts that the Secretary-General, in the context of the ongoing UN80 Initiative, will articulate a clearer strategic framework for identifying opportunities for consolidation of United Nations presence, in particular where multiple entities coexist, and for further rationalization of functions, in particular of senior and high-level positions required in special political missions with a smaller footprint, and for strengthened synergies among entities, including clear delineation of roles to be performed by the Missions and by the 25-16802 18/32 A/80/7/Add.10 Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs (see also A/80/7/Add.11, para. 8). The Committee considers that, in the context of constrained resources, efforts should be undertaken for comparative benchmarking among special political missions, enabling systematic assessment of their cost-effectiveness and comparative advantages in implementing mandates. (para. 48).

In the context of the UN80 Initiative, the report “Shifting the Paradigm: United to Deliver” outlines concrete steps towards a more streamlined and coherent field architecture. An initial set of measures has been advanced to consolidate and reconfigure selected presences, including: the integration of the United Nations Mission to Support the Hudaydah Agreement into the Office of the Special Envoy for Yemen, in line with Security Council resolution 2813 (2026); the closer alignment of the Mission of the Secretary-General’s Good Offices in Cyprus with the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, while preserving mandate delivery capacity; and the rationalization of the Office of the United Nations Representative to the Geneva International Discussions through optimized staffing and support structures. These measures, as articulated in the respective thematic cluster report reflect a broader shift towards more consolidated configurations, including the reduction of senior-level positions where appropriate.
Overall, the proposed budget for 2027 for special political missions reflects a total decrease of 4 high level posts (D-1 and above) comprising 1 USG, and 3 D-1 posts.

The Advisory Committee considers that the revised estimates for 2026 do not provide comprehensive information on the impact of proposed budget reductions in the implementation of mandates, or on the organizational structure of the special political missions. The Committee trusts that detailed informed in that regard will be provided to the General Assembly at the time of consideration of the present report. The Committee underscores the importance of adopting effective mitigation measures to offset the decreased level of resources and reduce any potential adverse impact on mandate delivery. The Committee trusts that information on the implementation of mandate, along with impact-oriented performance metrics in comparison to past performance, will be provided in the proposed programme budget for 2027 (para. 49).

Detailed information on the impact of the proposed reductions on mandate implementation has been provided to the Fifth Committee during its consideration of the revised estimates. The Secretariat will be further guided by General Assembly resolution A/RES/80/251 on mandate creation, implementation and review, with a view to ensuring a more efficient and effective United Nations.

Taking into account the proposals in both the proposed programme budget and the revised estimates for 2026, the Advisory Committee notes that the backstopping posts at Headquarters will be 34 as at 1 January 2026 and 31 as at 1 November 2026, compared with 40 posts approved for 2025. The Committee reiterates its expectation that consolidated information on backstopping positions at Headquarters will continue to be provided in future budget submissions. The Committee trusts that the existing backstopping positions at Headquarters will continue to be reviewed annually, on the basis of workload analysis, in order to realign the capacities when changes in the mandates of the missions occur with a view to achieving more efficiency in backstopping support (see A/79/7/Add.1, para. 54) (para. 54).
Information on resources for backstopping is provided in paragraphs 137 to 141 with more detailed information included in the supplementary information package.

The Advisory Committee is of the view that, with the provision of full suite of services to the 10 clients who previously received only payroll and education grant services, administrative capacities in those 10 special political missions must be reviewed for possible streamlining and trusts that information and proposals in that regard will be provided in the next report. (para. 56).
Following the transition of KJSO clients to the RSCE, the Center will not be providing the full suite of services to all clients at this stage.

With the closure of the Kuwait Joint Support Office as of 30 June 2026, the Advisory Committee welcomes the proposed transfer of the client missions of the Support Office to the Regional Service Centre in Entebbe. The Committee trusts that the transfer will be well planned and coordinated under the leadership of the Department of Operational Support, with adequate resource planning and operational readiness, to ensure a seamless takeover of client missions and timely delivery of services. The Committee trusts that the impact on service provision to new client entities will be monitored and reported, to better assess both efficiencies and improvements in support to clients, and to track the challenges experienced in the process, to facilitate the adoption of mitigation measures, as appropriate (para. 58).

The Secretariat acknowledges the Committee’s observations regarding the transfer of KJSO client missions to the Regional Service Centre in Entebbe and affirms that the transition is being executed pursuant to a structured, risk‑based framework designed to ensure continuity of operations and adherence to established service standards. The phased sequencing of functions, supported by joint planning, parallel servicing arrangements, defined hyper‑care periods, and retained fallback capacity, is underpinned by robust governance through a dedicated transition oversight team and continuous performance monitoring using key performance indicators, consolidated risk registers, and strengthened internal controls. The RSCE will continue to systematically monitor and report on the impact of the transition on service provision—supported by enhanced feedback mechanisms and change‑management measures—ensuring that efficiencies, challenges, and required mitigation actions are transparently captured as RSCE assumes full responsibility for the expanded client base in accordance with its established shared‑services model.

The Advisory Committee trusts that special political missions will limit new acquisition of new vehicles and laptops, as possible, before undertaking the indicated comprehensive review of the composition of their ground fleet and laptop holdings in view of the reduced footprint, and that information on efficiencies achieved in that regard will be included in the next budget (para. 65).

For 2027, proposed acquisitions for new vehicles or equipment are made following a careful review of the Mission’s staffing levels and operational needs. Where such needs were identified, Missions were required to pprioritizing the use of existing assets, including the United Nations Reserve, strategic deployment stocks (SDS), the return, refurbishment and reuse programme (3R), and identified surplus property from other entities, prior to proposing the procurement of new item.  
In UNSCOL, efficiencies amounting to $438,100 were achieved through cost avoidance related to the non-acquisition of vehicles, equipment or supplies owing to the transfer of assets from UNIFIL in UNSCOL.

The Advisory Committee, while acknowledging specific requirements in field operations, highlights that most of the deviations arise from areas for which the Standard Cost and Ratio Manual does not provide guidance or specify ratios (see para. 67 above). The Committee recalls that the General Assembly expressed concern about the significant variance between the actual vehicle and computing device holdings and standard allocations in special political missions, and in this regard requested the Secretary-General to update the vehicle holding ratio and related guidance, as well as the computing device allocation ratio (in a way that allows the ratios to be relevant), to enable the missions to improve the transparency and accuracy of the relevant budget (see resolution 79/258 A). (para. 69).

The Vehicle Ratios previously developed require updates to ensure they remain relevant and reflect current realities, such as the need for vehicles for national staff and experts (in sanctions panels), and the categorization of duty stations which may give rise to varying safety and security requirements.  Subject to availability of resources, the Secretariat will undertake a comprehensive assessment of client needs to ensure that the resulting ratios effectively support the implementation of their respective mandates.
OICT has updated the distribution ratios of computing devices to better reflect realistic device allocations and identified areas and staff categories where additional computing devices may be required.  This is communicated as part of the annual ICT budget guidelines to all field entities.

The Advisory Committee has expressed the view that it considers there is a need to enhance the performance information, including construction projects, for field-based special political missions under thematic cluster III (A/78/7/Add.1, para. 56; see also para. 58 above). The Committee concurs with the Board of Auditors on the need for more detailed information on construction projects in budget submissions and trusts that the recommendation of the Board of Auditors will be implemented expeditiously as soon as possible (para. 70).
Information on the efforts of the Secretariat to improve the presentation of financial performance, including construction projects is provided in paragraphs 18-119.

The Advisory Committee notes with concern that the requested information on annual appointments to geographical posts by special political missions, as endorsed by the General Assembly in its resolution 79/258 A, was not provided in the budget submission for 2026, and reiterates that information on annual appointments to geographical posts by mission, level, nationality and representation status should be provided in future budget submissions for the special political missions, with the information from 1 January to 31 December 2025 in the proposed programme budget for 2027 (see A/79/7/Add.1, para. 72)  (para. 71).
Information on on annual appointments to geographical posts by special political missions is provided in the supplementary information package.

The Advisory Committee notes with concern that, during 2024, the first year since the widening of the posts subject to the desirable ranges system to all posts funded by the regular budget at the Professional and higher categories, including in special political missions, 40.8 per cent of the total appointments and reassignments with geographical status were nationals of overrepresented Member States, while only 20 per cent were of underrepresented Member States. The Committee recalls that the Assembly, in its resolution 77/278, encouraged the Secretary-General to work towards bringing each unrepresented and underrepresented Member State within its desirable range by 2030 and endorsed the recommendations of the Committee, which underscored that additional efforts are needed for progress to be achieved (see A/80/7, para. 52).  (para. 72).

The Secretariat acknowledges the Advisory Committee’s observation and recognizes that improving geographical balance requires sustained and coordinated efforts. A key challenge remains the limited number of applications from nationals of unrepresented and underrepresented Member States.
To address this, the Secretariat is strengthening targeted outreach through partnerships with Member States, universities, professional networks, and the broader UN country presence, including Resident Coordinators and UN Information Centres. It is also developing purposeful partnerships to build sustainable talent pipelines and support candidates through capacity-development initiatives that improve their preparedness for UN recruitment processes.
At the same time, reforms under Staff Selection programme 2.0 aim to enhance transparency, efficiency, and skills-based recruitment, while improving access and fairness in selection processes. The Secretariat also notes that progress depends on adequate financial resources, as liquidity constraints can affect the timely filling of posts.
Through strengthened outreach, recruitment reforms, strategic partnerships with Member States, and adequate resources, the Secretariat aims to achieve sustained progress toward equitable geographical distribution.
